name: Singed Squire
text: A squire sits on an upturned helmet with a shield across his knees. He has no eyebrows. The shield is scorched black on the front, and so is most of the squire. "Do not," he says, before you can ask, "chase the bull. If you meet a shaggy bull with a horse's mane and horns that curl right back on themselves, you will think: those horns are useless, I will chase it. Do not."

options.label: Ask what the bull did
options.outcome: "It ran away," he says with dignity. "And as it ran it defended itself. From the back. Across the whole width of the room. The bestiary calls the beast a bonnacon and I call it a disgrace. My master is having a bath. He has been having it since yesterday."
options.chronicle: A squire with no eyebrows warned me about a bull called a bonnacon.

options.label: Give him something to eat and hear the rest
options.outcome: He eats like a man who has been living on pride. "It lairs a floor or two below here, some seasons. Cold slows it. Get close before it turns round, or keep a wall between you and its hindquarters. And take this; my master says he never wants to see a bottle again."
options.chronicle: Fed a squire with no eyebrows and heard the rest of the story about the bull. I will not be chasing any shaggy bulls.

road.hint: Never chase a bull whose best defence comes out of the back end.

options.label: Leave him to his scorch marks
options.outcome: "From the back!" he calls after you. "Remember that!"

name: Gikk
text: A small goblin huddles in the corner, shaking. It holds up a shiny trinket in trembling claws. "No hurt! No hurt! Gikk trade! Gikk give shiny for not-stabbing!"

options.label: Accept the trinket
options.outcome: Gikk shoves the trinket into your hands and scrambles away, disappearing into a crack in the wall you didn't notice before. The trinket is surprisingly well-made.

options.label: Give Gikk some food
options.outcome: Gikk's eyes go wide. "Food? FOOD! Gikk never get food-gift before!" He shoves the trinket at you and produces a second one from somewhere unspeakable. "Two shinies! For food-friend!" You receive two items.
options.chronicle: Fed a frightened goblin named Gikk. He gave me a trinket and ran.

road.hint: A frightened goblin pays in whatever is in his pocket.

options.label: Shoo him away
options.outcome: Gikk yelps and bolts, taking his shiny with him. You hear tiny footsteps fading into the dark, followed by what might be sobbing.

name: Very Small Rat King
text: Three rats with their tails knotted together regard you from atop a small cairn of pebbles. The middle one wears a bottle cap on its head like a crown. It squeaks at you with evident authority. The other two squeak in apparent agreement. They seem to be negotiating something.

options.label: Offer them some food
options.outcome: The Rat King accepts your offering with regal dignity. After a brief three-way consultation, one rat produces a small pile of coins from somewhere in the cairn and nudges them toward you. You have apparently satisfied a trade agreement.

options.label: Bow to the Rat King
options.outcome: All three rats sit up very straight. The crowned rat touches its bottle cap with one tiny paw, a gesture of unmistakable royal acknowledgment. A curious lightness fills your legs. The court of the Rat King has blessed your passage.
options.chronicle: Bowed to a king of three rats. He accepted graciously.

road.hint: Even a very small king expects a bow.

options.label: Leave the rats to their politics
options.outcome: The Rat King watches you go with the cool, assessing gaze of a monarch who has seen many adventurers pass and will see many more. The squeaking resumes behind you, businesslike.

name: Wat Rowe
text: An old man sits on a step with a lamp-pole across his knees and a flask of oil in his lap, getting his breath back for the third time. Six lamps burn on the stair above him, one to a landing. Below, the Long Stair goes on down through floor after floor, and it is dark. "Six," he says. "I've done six. The seventh's at the very bottom, a few floors down yet, and my knees have stopped speaking to me." He holds up the flask. "Would you? It's on your way. It's on everybody's way. That's the point of it."

options.label: Take his oil and swear to light the seventh lamp
options.outcome: He gives you the flask as if it were an heirloom, which it is. "Don't let it go out," he says. "Nobody remembers who lit a lamp. Everybody remembers falling."

oath.what: Light the seventh lamp at the foot of the Long Stair.

thread.hint: A cold lamp waits at the foot of the Long Stair.

options.chronicle: Promised an old lamplighter named Wat that I would light the seventh lamp at the bottom of the stair. He gave me his oil like an heirloom.

road.hint: Nobody remembers who lit a lamp. Everybody remembers falling.

options.label: Carry him down a flight to wake his knees
options.outcome: He weighs nothing and complains the whole way. You carry him down one flight to the next lamp-post and back up, and by the top his knees have started speaking to him again. "That's the worst of it done," he says. "I'll take the rest slow. A floor at a time."
options.chronicle: Carried an old lamplighter down a flight of his own stair and back up, to wake his knees. He means to take the rest of the way down himself, slowly.

road.hint: Some old men would rather be carried than replaced.

options.label: Wish him well and go on
options.outcome: "Well," he says. "Maybe the knees will speak to me tomorrow." He gets his breath back for the fourth time.

name: Young Scribe
text: A nervous young man in scholar's robes clutches a leather satchel and an extinguished lantern, squinting in the dark. "I'm documenting dungeon fauna for the Cartographers' Guild," he explains. "My torch went out and I haven't seen anything worth writing down yet. Could you... describe what you've encountered? I can pay per entry."

options.label: Describe creatures you've fought (spend SP)
options.outcome: He writes at furious speed, interrupting every sentence with clarifying questions about mandibles and preferred habitats. "Extraordinary. Just extraordinary." He counts out coins carefully. "Most adventurers just say 'it was big '."
options.chronicle: Described monsters to a nervous young scribe for his guild. He wrote 'enormous' a great deal.

road.hint: Every monster grows in the retelling.

options.label: Share food for his journey
options.outcome: He accepts the food with profound relief and rummages gratefully in his satchel. "Take this, I copied it in the library and already have the original. Genuine dungeon scholarship, not the popular stuff."

options.label: Point him toward the exit
options.outcome: He looks torn between relief and professional disappointment. "Perhaps... yes, perhaps that's sensible." He writes one final note, adds a small asterisk, and shuffles off toward the surface with his satchel held tight.

name: Old Traveler

tells: one eye is bright; the other is hidden

text: An old man in a grey cloak and a broad-brimmed hat sits on a rock by a dry well, leaning on a spear like a walking staff. One eye is bright; the other is hidden under the brim. Two ravens sit on the beam above, watching you, then him, as if taking notes. "A long road down," he says, in a voice like distant thunder. "Have you anything for an old wanderer's supper?" When he shifts on the rock, his boots make no sound at all.

options.label: Share food with him
options.outcome: He eats slowly and talks about wells: which are deep, which are worth what they cost to drink from. When you look up from your own bread, the ravens are gone, and so is he.
options.chronicle: Fed an old man with one eye. He talked about wells. His birds took notes.

road.hint: An old man who talks about wells may know the price of a drink.

options.label: Ask what he paid for his drink at the well

pass.outcome: He laughs like a thunderclap, a long way off. "An eye, and cheap at the price. Mimir would like you." He presses a thumb to your brow.
pass.chronicle: Asked an old man in a broad hat about a well. He knew exactly which well. I think I know now whose hat it was.

fail.outcome: "Water is water," he says, and is somehow already gone.

road.hint: Some questions only make sense if you noticed what was missing.

options.label: "You aren't a wanderer at all, are you, Grandfather?"
options.outcome: He tips the hat back. The other eye is not there. "Wanderer, Grey-Cloak, Hanged One. I have more names than teeth." He stands, and he is taller than the corridor ought to allow. "Mimir's Well is below you, if you want to know what wisdom costs. And mind the giant who likes riddles."
options.chronicle: Called the old wanderer by his true name. He did not deny it. Ravens followed me for a floor.

road.hint: A god in a borrowed hat likes being recognised more than being fed.

options.label: "I need my supplies."
options.outcome: "Of course," he says. "Supplies are what keep a man alive, until they don't." The ravens mutter to each other.

name: Wandering Herbalist
text: A small, wiry woman moves along the wall with a lantern, peering at patches of fungus with a jeweler's loupe. She barely glances at you. "I'm cataloguing. Don't touch the blue ones, they'll numb your tongue for a week. Are you interested in supplies, or are you just going to hover?"

options.label: Trade food for one of her potions
options.outcome: She accepts your ration with a professional nod and presses a small stoppered vial into your hand. "My morning's brew. I trust the apothecaria more than I trust the labels. Drink with caution."
options.chronicle: Traded food with a herbalist who warned me off the blue mushrooms. I believe her.

road.hint: Don't touch the blue ones.

options.label: Buy a restorative potion (45g)
options.outcome: She produces a small clay bottle and watches you drink it with clinical interest. The warmth is immediate and genuine. "Bloodmoss and deep-cave ginger. Works on most species. You're welcome."

options.label: Leave her to her research
options.outcome: She has already forgotten you exist, loupe back against her eye, muttering notes to herself. The lantern light shrinks behind you as you walk on.

name: Brix
text: A goblin wearing a vest with far too many pockets materializes from behind a stalagmite, arms spread wide. "HELLO CUSTOMER! Brix has very good items! Definitely not cursed! Most of them! Best prices in dungeon, guaranteed by Brix personally!"

options.label: Buy his "special item" (20g)
options.outcome: Brix produces a small object from a pocket that shouldn't physically contain it, wrapped in what appears to be an old sock. "Is good! Brix promises! Mostly!" He vanishes before you can ask any follow-up questions.
options.chronicle: Bought something from a goblin named Brix who swore most of his stock was not cursed.

road.hint: Most of them is not all of them.

options.label: Buy a wand from him (40g)
options.outcome: "Ooh, fancy customer wants fancy item!" Brix digs through several pockets before retrieving a wand with a slight scorch mark on one end. "Barely used! Only misfired twice!"

options.label: "No thank you, Brix."
options.outcome: Brix looks genuinely wounded. "No customer? But Brix had such good deals today..." He retreats behind the stalagmite with a tragic little sigh. You feel slightly guilty.

name: Barnaby Thrupp, Lost Merchant
text: A portly man with a tipped-over handcart blocks the corridor, muttering furiously as he tries to restack a pile of rolled-up maps. "Thirty years in the trade and I still can't read these wretched things! You there, maybe we can help each other out?"

options.label: Buy a potion from him (30g)
options.outcome: He rummages through the cart with suspicious enthusiasm and produces a bottle from somewhere near the bottom. "Best stock in the dungeon! Probably. Good luck, friend."
options.chronicle: Bought supplies from a lost merchant who cannot read his own maps. He was very cheerful about it.

road.hint: A merchant who cannot read maps sells them anyway.

options.label: Buy a scroll from him (25g)
options.outcome: He slaps a rolled scroll into your hand with the confidence of a man who has no idea what it does. "Guaranteed authentic. Mostly. Probably."

options.label: Trade food for a random potion
options.outcome: "Pleasure doing business." He wraps the potion carefully and hands it over.

options.label: Leave him to his maps
options.outcome: He waves you off without looking up, already arguing with the map under his breath. You walk on, accompanied by the fading sound of someone losing a debate with parchment.

name: Baucis and Philemon

tells: a grey-bearded giant of a man
two small pinions in his hatband

text: An old man and an old woman have made a home of an alcove: one stool, one pot, one very suspicious goose. Two travellers already crowd the table, a grey-bearded giant of a man and a young one with two small pinions in his hatband. "More guests," says the woman, delighted. They have half an onion and a heel of bread between them all, and they are setting it in front of you. The pitcher of thin wine has been poured a dozen times. It is still full.

options.label: Eat what they offer; refusing would shame them
options.outcome: It is the best half onion you have ever eaten. They watch every bite with delight and go to bed hungry, which they are used to.
options.chronicle: An old couple gave me their whole supper, and I ate it, and they were delighted.

road.hint: A poor man's supper eaten gladly is a gift returned.

options.label: Put your own food on the table and share it out
options.outcome: Five at a table laid for one. The old man tells how they met and the old woman corrects him. The grey-bearded guest laughs so hard the wall creaks.
options.chronicle: Shared my rations at an old couple's table with two strangers. The big one laughed so hard the wall creaked.

road.hint: Bread shared at a poor table is never only bread.

options.label: Look at the pitcher, then at the grey-bearded guest

pass.outcome: You watch the pitcher fill itself as the old woman pours. You look up, and the grey-bearded guest is looking right back at you, and his eyes are the colour of a summer storm. He puts a finger to his lips. Then he turns to the old couple. "You have been kind to strangers. Ask for anything." They look at each other. "Let neither of us have to bury the other," says Philemon. The young guest with the winged hat winks at you.
pass.chronicle: Noticed the pitcher at an old couple's table never emptied, and the guest who noticed me noticing. They asked to die on the same day. He said yes.

fail.outcome: You see a very good pitcher and two large strangers. The young one steals your spoon, you think.

road.hint: A pitcher that never empties is telling you who is at the table.

options.label: Offer to catch the goose for their pot
options.outcome: In the old story that goose outran two gods. It outruns you. The old couple applaud the attempt, and the goose settles back on its stool, looking vindicated. The grey-bearded guest is wiping his eyes.
options.chronicle: Chased an old couple's goose round an alcove. The goose won. A large stranger cried laughing.

road.hint: Some geese are protected by the guests.

name: Wynn the Pilgrim
text: A young woman in travelling robes sits against the wall with her boot off and her ankle swollen to the size of an apple. Her torch sputters. She holds a wooden rosary that is clearly not hers; the beads are worn smooth by someone else's thumb. "It's my mother's. She always meant to take it to the Shrine of the Deep, and she never got round to it." She tries to stand, and can't. "Could you walk with me to the next stair?"

on_arrive.outcome: At the stair she touches the rosary to your forehead. 'Mum would have liked you. She liked people who walked slowly.'
on_arrive.chronicle: Walked a pilgrim named Wynn to the stair at the pace of her bad ankle. She blessed me with her mother's rosary.

on_fail.chronicle: Lost Wynn the pilgrim on the way to the stair. Her mother's rosary is somewhere on this floor. I looked.

options.label: Walk her to the next stair
options.outcome: She leans on your arm. She weighs nothing, and talks all the way.

road.hint: Walking slowly beside someone is a kind of strength.

options.label: Give her food for the walk
options.outcome: She eats, thanks you, and limps on alone, very slowly.

options.label: Wish her well and move on
options.outcome: "God will provide," she says. "I suppose." She sounds less sure than she would like.

name: Osric the Mapmaker
text: A lean, precise man paces the corridor with a measuring cord, muttering dimensions under his breath and marking them on a chart stretched over a portable board. He notices you and taps the map. "You've been deeper than me today. I can pay for information. Distances, junctions, any notable features. What do you say?"

options.label: Share what you've seen (costs SP)
options.outcome: You spend twenty minutes walking him through everything you remember: every junction, chamber, and passage. He transcribes with incredible speed, humming approvingly. "Excellent recall. Here, fair compensation for your time and memory."
options.chronicle: Traded what I had seen for a copy of a mapmaker's chart. He measured me while we talked.

road.hint: A map is a trade of what each of you has seen.

options.label: Buy a copy of his current map (50g)
options.outcome: He produces a crisp, annotated copy with confident strokes. Studying it, you find that his spatial sense is almost preternatural, the layout settles in your mind like something you already knew.

options.label: Decline and continue on
options.outcome: He shrugs and returns to his measuring. "Another time, perhaps." You hear him muttering new distances as you round the corner, already absorbed in the architecture.

name: Saint Martin
text: When you next rest, at the foot of the stair, you dream of a man in half a cloak, standing among a crowd of angels. He is wearing your half. He turns it so they can see the cut edge. "Look," he says to them. "This is how I was clothed today."

options.label: Wake
options.outcome: You wake with your armour whole again and warm, as if someone had been wearing it.
options.chronicle: Dreamed of a man wearing the half of my cloak I gave away. Woke with my armour whole and warm. I have decided not to think too hard about it.

road.hint: Half a cloak given away is sometimes worn by someone you would not expect.

name: Tilly Hollins
text: A child, perhaps eight years old, sits in the middle of the corridor holding a lantern and eating an apple with great contentment. She looks up at you with complete composure. "Hello. Are you lost? I know all the paths on this level. My dad's a miner. I'm not supposed to be here but he doesn't know yet."

text_variants.text: A child, perhaps eight years old, sits in the middle of the corridor holding a lantern and eating an apple with great contentment. She looks up at you with complete composure. "Hello. Are you lost? I know all the paths on this level. My dad's a miner. I'm not supposed to be here but he doesn't know yet." "Have you seen my brother Davy anywhere?"

options.label: Share food and ask about the layout
options.outcome: You trade her a ration for ten minutes of the most thorough dungeon briefing you have ever received, complete with hand gestures. She describes three shortcuts, two trapped passages, and a very large rat she has named Gerald. You feel oddly well-oriented.
options.chronicle: A miner's girl named Tilly showed me the paths on her floor, with hand gestures. She has named a rat Gerald.

road.hint: A child who knows the paths knows who walked them.

outcome_variants.outcome: You trade her a ration for ten minutes of the most thorough dungeon briefing you have ever received, complete with hand gestures. She describes three shortcuts, two trapped passages, and a very large rat she has named Gerald. You feel oddly well-oriented.
outcome_variants.chronicle: A miner's girl named Tilly showed me the paths on her floor. She asked if I'd seen her brother.

options.label: Just share food, she should eat
options.outcome: She accepts solemnly, wraps it in her apron, and pats it. "For later. My dad says never eat the dungeon mushrooms unless Mrs. Herbst checks them first." She seems very wise for eight. You hope she finds her way home.

options.label: Tell her to go home
options.outcome: "I will in a minute," she says, not moving. You walk on with the unsettling feeling that she has been here longer than you, understands this place better than you do, and will leave exactly when she decides to.

name: Hob Tanner
text: A mill wheel turning in an underground race, flour in the air, and a big man with a bigger thumb weighing a widow's sack. The scale says less than the sack does; anyone watching closely can see the thumb. He sees you see it, and winks. "Gleaners don't check. Tell you what, friend. Three loaves for the price of one, and you never saw a thing." The widow, Gyda Fenn, is counting her coppers and not looking up. "It's always light in the autumn," she says, to nobody. "The damp gets in the grain."

options.label: Take the cheap bread and say nothing
options.outcome: He wraps the loaves in a cloth that has flour on it from everyone else's grain. The widow takes her short measure home.
options.chronicle: Bought three cheap loaves from a miller who weighs with his thumb. The bread is very good. Some widow paid for part of it.

road.hint: Cheap bread is sometimes paid for by someone else.

options.label: Tell the widow about his thumb
options.outcome: Gyda looks at the scale, and at the thumb, and then at Hob, for a long time. Then she calls the other gleaners over, all of them, and they stand round the scale with their arms folded while he weighs every sack again. His sons walk you to the door, firmly.
options.chronicle: Told a gleaner the miller had his thumb on the scale. The widows stood round his scale with their arms folded. His sons threw me out. Worth it.

road.hint: A thumb on a scale is easy to see if anybody looks.

options.label: Make up the widow's short measure from your own purse
options.warning: The scale says less than the sack does; anyone watching closely can see the thumb.
options.outcome: She thanks you, puzzled. Hob grins and weighs the next widow's sack with the same thumb. You cannot pay for all of them.
options.chronicle: Made up one widow's short measure out of my own purse. The miller weighed the next widow the same way. I cannot pay for all of them.

road.hint: Paying for a cheat's victims keeps the cheat in business.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Hob winks at you again as you go. The widow goes on counting her coppers.

name: Tibbet, Apprentice Alchemist
text: A teenager with singed eyebrows and ink-stained fingers sits beside a portable burner, three potions bubbling at once. "Oh thank goodness, a real person! I need a field tester. These should be fine. Probably. My master always said the second batch is the dangerous one, and this is the third, so statistically..."

options.label: Volunteer as test subject
options.outcome: The potion tastes like burnt copper and optimism. You experience a brief, intense sensation of being a slightly different shape, and then it passes. The apprentice scribbles in his notebook furiously. "Fascinating! Here, take the good one as payment."
options.chronicle: Tested a teenage alchemist's potion for her. I still have both my eyebrows, which is more than she has.

road.hint: The second batch is always the dangerous one.

options.label: Buy a tested potion (35g)
options.outcome: "This one I'm fairly confident about," he says, handing you a blue vial. "Only about a fifteen percent chance of anything unusual. Which is actually very good for my batch size!"

options.label: "Best of luck with your research."
options.outcome: He looks disappointed but philosophical. "Fair enough. Not everyone has the spirit of scientific inquiry." One of his potions chooses this moment to turn bright purple. He stares at it. "That's... new."

name: The Seventh Lamp
text: At the foot of a long stair stands an iron post with an empty lamp-cup on top, and six lamps lit on the steps above it, each one of Wat's, each one still burning. The seventh cup is cold. Below it, scratched in the iron: FOR THEM AS COME DOWN AFTER. The stair below is very dark, and so is this whole floor: your own light is guttering, and Wat's flask is the only good oil you have.

options.label: Fill the cup with Wat's oil and light it
options.outcome: The wick takes at once, as if it had been waiting. The light goes down the stair much further than a lamp that size should reach. Somewhere above, very faint, a bell rings once.
options.chronicle: Lit the seventh lamp at the foot of the long stair, as I told old Wat I would. The light went further down than a lamp should.

road.hint: A lamp lit for strangers lights your own feet first.

options.label: "I lost Wat's oil."
options.outcome: You say it out loud to the cold cup, because there is no one else to say it to. The stair below stays dark. Somewhere above, an old man is still listening for a bell.
options.chronicle: Reached the seventh lamp without Wat's oil. I had lost it on the way down. The cup is still cold, and I said so to it.

road.hint: Oil promised to a lamp is owed even after the flask is gone.

options.label: Keep the oil for your own light
options.outcome: Your own light burns brighter and warmer for floors. The seventh cup stays cold behind you, and the stair below it stays dark for whoever comes next.
options.chronicle: Burned old Wat's lamp oil to light my own way. The seventh cup is still cold. My own way has never been so bright.

road.hint: Oil promised to a public lamp burns oddly in a private one.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The seventh cup stays cold behind you.

text_variants.text: At the foot of a long stair stands an iron post with an empty lamp-cup on top, and six lamps lit on the steps above it, each one of Wat's, each one still burning. The seventh cup is cold. Below it, scratched in the iron: FOR THEM AS COME DOWN AFTER. The stair below is very dark, and so is this whole floor: your own light is guttering, and Wat's flask is no longer in your pack.

name: Luminous Mushrooms
text: Three enormous mushrooms glow with a soft violet light in a side alcove, their caps pulsing in slow rhythm. As you approach, you become aware, without quite knowing how, that they are curious about you. Not dangerous. Just... attentive. One tilts, slightly, in your direction.

options.label: Eat a small piece of one
options.outcome: The taste is cold and electric and somehow also the color blue. Your vision doubles briefly, filling with slow purple geometries, and then clears. Your mind feels extraordinarily clean, like a window after rain.

options.label: Sit in their light for a while
options.outcome: You rest in the gentle pulse of their glow. There is something profoundly calm about being near something that has no fear of the dungeon, that simply exists and grows and shines. You feel your hurts ease, just slightly.
options.chronicle: Sat in the light of three curious mushrooms. They were curious about me. I felt better.

road.hint: Some things in the dark are only curious.

options.label: Leave them in peace
options.outcome: The mushrooms watch you go with whatever sense they use for watching. The violet glow lingers at the edge of your vision for some time, a small and patient light in the dark.

name: Crying Girl
text: A small girl sits in the mouth of a side passage, sobbing as if her heart would break. "My da's hurt, he's just in there, please, please come." Her hands are clean. Her tears have left no tracks in the soot on her cheeks. In the dust behind her, big boot prints go into the dark and don't come out.

options.label: Go with her to help her da
options.warning: Her tears have left no tracks in the soot on her cheeks.
options.outcome: Three steps into the dark a club finds the back of your head. When you can see again your purse is lighter and two men are coming back for the rest. Somewhere behind them a man laughs and says, "Good girl, Wren."
options.chronicle: Followed a crying girl into a side passage to help her father. Her father was two men with clubs, and a third who laughed. They called her a good girl.

road.hint: Tears that leave no tracks were never cried.

options.label: Look harder before you go in

pass.outcome: No tracks through the soot. Clean hands. Boots in, none out. You go round by the other passage and come up behind three men crouched in the dark with clubs, waiting for the girl's next customer. They are not ready for you. Afterwards Wren sits on a rock and stares at you. "They took me off a caravan," she says. "They said they'd sell me if I didn't cry good." You point her to the stair. She goes, then comes back for the wreckers' purse, then goes.
pass.chronicle: Saw through a crying girl's trap, came up behind the men who set it, and sent her home. Her name is Wren. She cries very well.

fail.outcome: You look, and see only a crying child. You go in.
fail.chronicle: Looked hard at a crying girl and saw only a crying girl. It cost me my purse.

road.hint: Before you follow a cry into the dark, look at the floor.

options.label: Throw her a coin and walk on
options.outcome: She catches it without looking, the way only practised hands do.
options.chronicle: Threw a coin to a crying girl and kept walking. She caught it like a professional, which in a way she was.

road.hint: Practised hands catch coins without looking.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The crying stops the moment you are past. Then, after a moment, it starts again, for someone else.

name: Drowned Girl
text: A girl of about nine sits on a stone step at the edge of black water, wet through, holding out an empty hand. An old ferryman leans on his oar a little way off. "No coin, no crossing. Rules." The girl says, "My stepfather kept my coin. He said the dead don't need money." She has been sitting here, the ferryman mentions, since the reign of a king nobody remembers.

options.label: Pay her fare
options.outcome: Charon bites the coin, nods, and holds out a hand for her. She stops on the ferry and waves at you until the dark takes the boat.
options.chronicle: Paid a drowned girl's fare across the black water. Her stepfather kept her coin. She waved until the dark took the boat.

road.hint: A coin for a stranger's crossing is a small coin with a long memory.

pass.outcome: You point out that the rule says a coin, not whose coin, and that he has already been paid in the waiting. He grumbles, and takes half a fare from you, and lets her on.
pass.chronicle: Argued the letter of the rule with Charon until he took a drowned girl across for half fare. He grumbled the whole time.

fail.outcome: "Rules," says Charon.

road.hint: A rule followed past the point of sense is still followed by someone.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: She keeps holding her hand out, to the next person.

name: Desperate Treasure-Hunter
text: A man stumbles toward you from the shadows, clutching a rough map to his chest. His gear is expensive but battered, and he has the look of someone who has been underground too long. "Please. I've found something, a cache, two junctions east, but there's something guarding it. I need what you have more than you do right now."

options.label: Sell him a potion (take 50g)
options.outcome: You hand him a potion and he gives you coin with trembling hands, already moving. "You've saved my life. I'll remember this." He rounds the corner at speed. You never do find out if he was right about the cache.

options.label: Give him food from your pack
options.outcome: His face crumples with relief. "Here, I can't use this, my hands shake too much to read it properly." He presses a scroll into your hands and takes off down the corridor without another word.
options.chronicle: Sold a desperate treasure-hunter food at a fair price. He thought it was a terrible price.

road.hint: A starving man and a fair price are rarely friends.

options.label: Wish him luck and move on
options.outcome: He stares at you for a moment, then nods with quiet dignity. "Right. Fair enough. Every man for himself down here." He straightens his coat and walks east, toward whatever is waiting for him.

name: The Singing Bones
text: A neat pile of bones in the corner of a chamber is, unmistakably, humming. As you draw closer, a dry voice rises from the heap: "I know that tread. Another seeker. I've been here a hundred years and I've seen your type come and go. Ask your question. I'm not going anywhere."

options.label: Ask about dangers ahead
options.outcome: The bones clatter softly as they consider their price. You leave the gold on the floor. "Mm. Fair." A dry whisper fills your mind with echoes of corridors and shadows, you feel briefly aware of things just beyond your sight.
options.chronicle: Asked a pile of bones about the road ahead. It hummed while it answered.

road.hint: The dead are good at directions; they have had time.

options.label: Ask how they died
options.outcome: "Overconfidence," the bones say without hesitation. "Same as most of you. I had a enchanted sword and a plan and absolutely no idea what was waiting on level twelve." A pause. "Don't make my mistake."

options.label: Walk away from the talking bones
options.outcome: "Rude," the bones observe, as you leave. The humming resumes behind you, a slow and sourceless melody that follows you down the corridor for longer than it should.

name: Moneylender's Purse
text: You find a fat purse in the dust with FISK stitched on it. Inside: gold, and eleven folded debt markers with miners' marks on them. A wheezing man in a good coat comes back down the corridor, searching. "My purse. Ottokar Fisk. I lent to those families when no bank on Gullet Row would." A widow follows at a distance. "A fifth a month," she says. "My husband signed it drunk." Fisk doesn't turn round. "He signed it sober, and asked me twice."

options.label: Give Fisk his purse, markers and all
options.outcome: He counts it in front of you, which is rude, and then gives you a single coin, which is ruder. The widow watches the markers go back into his coat.
options.chronicle: Gave a moneylender back his purse, debts and all. He tipped me one coin. The widow behind him did not tip me anything.

road.hint: A lost purse belongs to its owner, even an owner you dislike.

options.label: Keep the gold. Give the widow her husband's marker
options.outcome: Agna takes the marker and folds it very small and puts it inside her dress. "Thank you," she says, and means it. Fisk is still searching up the corridor, wheezing, and does not look back.

delayed.text: A notice on a stair-post in Fisk's square hand: NO MORE LOANS ON GULLET ROW. THIEVES ABOUT.

options.chronicle: Kept a moneylender's gold and gave a widow back her husband's debt. She thanked me. Fisk has stopped lending on Gullet Row.

road.hint: A gift made from someone else's purse is still paid by someone.

options.label: Burn the markers and give him back the gold
options.warning: I lent to those families when no bank on Gullet Row would.
options.outcome: The markers go up in a pretty little flame. Agna cries. Fisk takes his gold back with shaking hands and says, very quietly, "Then I'll lend to nobody."

delayed.text: A miner's lad stops you on the stair. 'Fisk stopped lending after his markers burned. Nobody else will. Mam couldn't buy her seed.' He has no idea it was you.

options.chronicle: Burned a moneylender's debt markers and gave him his gold back. The widow cried. Fisk says he will lend to nobody now. I believe him.

road.hint: Burn the lender's books and the next loan burns with them.

options.label: Leave the purse where it fell
options.outcome: You walk on. Behind you, while Fisk's back is turned, the widow gets to it first.
options.chronicle: Left a moneylender's purse lying in the road for its owner, or for whoever got there first.

road.hint: A choice left on the floor goes to the next person along.

name: Moaning Woman
text: A woman is slumped against the wall, moaning in pain. Her long dark hair hangs over her face, and her body shudders with each ragged breath. One hand clutches her stomach. She doesn't look up as you approach. The moaning has a rhythm to it, like somebody counting.

options.label: Kneel down and try to help her
options.warning: The moaning has a rhythm to it, like somebody counting.
options.outcome: You reach out to move her hair aside, and her head snaps up. The face underneath is grey and rotting, the eyes pure white. "I'LL SWALLOW YOUR SOUL!" she shrieks, and rakes you across the chest before you can react. She was dead the whole time.
options.chronicle: Knelt to help a moaning woman. She was a Deadite. She tried to swallow my soul. I have a scratch to remember her by.

road.hint: The moaning had a rhythm. The dead keep time.

options.label: "It's a trick. Axe out, or whatever you've got."

pass.outcome: You draw your weapon and come in sideways. The "woman" springs up with inhuman speed, grey flesh splitting into a horrible grin, but you were ready. One clean strike and it's over. You wipe your weapon clean. "Groovy."
pass.chronicle: Smelled a trick in a moaning woman and had my weapon out before she turned. Groovy.

fail.outcome: You're nearly ready. Nearly. She rakes you once on the way down.
fail.chronicle: Saw the Deadite coming and still let her get a claw in. Paranoia is only useful if it is quick.

road.hint: Good, bad: the one who wins is the one holding the axe first.

options.label: Say the words, to be sure. "Klaatu, Barada, N... Necktie."
options.outcome: You definitely said all of the words. Mostly. The floor cracks in two places and two more of them climb out to join her. You may have said a word wrong.
options.chronicle: Said the old words over a Deadite to keep the dead down. I said most of them. Two more climbed out. I am going to go with necktie.

road.hint: Some words have to be said exactly, or not at all.

options.label: Walk away and leave her be
options.outcome: You give the moaning figure a wide berth. As you round the corner, the moaning stops. When you glance back, she's gone.
options.chronicle: Walked past a moaning woman. The moaning stopped when I turned the corner. I did not go back to check why.

name: Freezing Beggar
text: A wind comes up the stair out of nowhere, colder than any wind should be underground, and at a stone gate a beggar sits curled against it, nearly naked and blue with cold. Everyone coming through the gate steps round him. Nobody looks. You have a cloak, and something with an edge.

options.label: Cut your cloak in half with whatever blade you carry, and give him half
options.outcome: The blade goes through the cloth cleanly. He wraps your half round his shoulders and looks up at you once, and you have the odd feeling he knows your name.
options.chronicle: Cut my cloak in half at a cold gate and gave half to a beggar. People laughed at the half I kept. He looked at me as if he knew my name.

road.hint: Half a cloak given is warmer than a whole one kept.

options.label: Give him food
options.outcome: He eats, shivering. It is not cold food he is dying of.
options.chronicle: Gave a freezing beggar food. He thanked me. He was still freezing.

road.hint: Feed the hungry man, clothe the cold one.

options.label: Step round him like everyone else

name: Broken Automaton
text: A copper-and-brass figure sits propped against a pillar, one arm missing, the clockwork of its chest exposed and still. Its glass eyes flicker. "My... purpose... incomplete," it says, in a voice like keys on a music box. "I was a guardian. I am not... I cannot fulfill... can you carry something? In my place?"

options.label: Accept its remaining charge (take damage)
options.outcome: It extends its remaining hand and something jumps between you like a static spark, sharp and cold. "Guardian's... charge... transferred. You will hold it better than I do now." Its glass eyes dim and it is still. You feel a faint hum of protection wrapped around you.
options.chronicle: Took the last charge of a broken guardian. It said its purpose was incomplete. So, I suppose, is mine.

road.hint: A guardian with no purpose left can still give one away.

options.label: Try to repair it (spend SP)
options.outcome: You work at the exposed clockwork, improvising where parts are missing. It won't walk again, but the chest plate closes and its eyes brighten. "Grateful," it says. "Gratitude... registered." A hidden compartment in its base clicks open, revealing a cache of coin.

options.label: Leave it to rest
options.outcome: "Understood," it says. "I will... wait." Its eyes dim to a faint flicker. You wonder how long it has already been waiting, and how much longer it will.

name: Old Nan and the Cat
text: A translucent figure sits cross-legged on the dungeon floor, head in her hands, softly crying. She looks up at your approach, her eyes are empty of color, her clothes decades out of fashion. "Oh. Another adventurer. Have you... have you seen my cat? His name is Cobbler. He was orange."

options.label: Sit with her for a while
options.outcome: You sit in companionable silence for a time. She doesn't speak again, but gradually her crying stills. When you rise to leave, she offers you a small, sad smile. Something about her quiet grief has steadied your own mind.
options.chronicle: Sat with an old ghost who has lost her cat. I did not tell her how long it has been.

road.hint: A ghost looking for a cat is looking for a reason to stay.

options.label: Tell her you haven't seen a cat
options.outcome: "He was very good at catching rats," she says softly. "He kept me company when the dungeon was quiet." She fades a little, looking past you. "It's very quiet now."

options.label: Walk away quietly
options.outcome: You slip past without a word. Behind you, the soft weeping resumes and then is swallowed by the dark. You don't look back.

name: Frozen Viper
text: In a cold side cave lies a snake as long as a man, stiff with cold, its zigzag back dull with frost. It lifts its head an inch. "Warm me," it whispers. "Inside your shirt. Just till I can move. I'm not that kind of snake." Its pupils are slits, and its head is the shape of a spade.

options.label: Warm it inside your shirt
options.warning: Its pupils are slits, and its head is the shape of a spade.
options.outcome: It warms quickly against you. Then it bites you, almost apologetically. "It's my nature," it says.
options.chronicle: Warmed a frozen viper in my shirt because it asked nicely. It bit me, and said it was its nature. The fable warned me. I had not read the fable.

road.hint: A snake that says it is not that kind of snake is that kind of snake.

options.label: Set it on the warm rock by your light, at arm's length

pass.outcome: You lift it with a stick, set it on the warm stone and step back well out of reach. It thaws, uncoils, and looks at you with something like respect. "Smart. I'd have bitten you. It's my nature." It tells you where a dead trapper left his purse.
pass.chronicle: Thawed a viper with a stick from a safe distance. It said it would have bitten me, and told me where to find a dead man's purse.

fail.outcome: You misjudge the stick.
fail.chronicle: Tried to thaw a viper from a safe distance. The distance was not safe.

road.hint: Help a viper from the length of a stick.

options.label: Leave it to the cold
options.outcome: "Sensible," it hisses. "I wouldn't warm me either."

name: Father of Three
text: A man in a once-fine coat sits outside a shut door, counting the same four coins over and over. Behind the door three girls are arguing in whispers about which of them should go into service with the goblin tallyman so the other two can eat. He has not noticed you. Above the door there is a gap about the width of a purse. One full purse would settle the whole debt.

options.label: Drop a purse through the gap and slip away
options.outcome: The purse lands with a clink that stops the argument dead. By the time the door opens you are round the corner. Nobody thanks you, because nobody knows. Bishop Nicholas of Myra gave this way on three separate nights, and the father only caught him on the third.
options.chronicle: Left a purse where a family would find it. They will never know whose.

road.hint: A gift with no name on it cannot be paid back, which is the point.

options.label: Put the gold in his hand and let him thank you
options.outcome: He weeps, calls his daughters out to curtsey, and presses his late wife's ring on you. He will not hear no. The girls look at the floor the whole time. It is a good ring.
options.chronicle: Paid a stranger's debt and was thanked for it at length. His daughters curtseyed. They did not look up.

road.hint: Thanks taken in front of children is paid for by the children.

options.label: Walk on; your own purse is thin enough
options.outcome: The whispering goes on behind the door. The man starts counting his four coins again from the beginning.
options.chronicle: Walked past a man counting four coins outside a door. He was still counting when I turned the corner.

road.hint: Four coins counted twice are still four coins.

name: Ornate Mirror
text: A full-length mirror stands inexplicably in the dungeon corridor, its silver frame carved with serpents eating their own tails. Your reflection stares back, a half-second too slow. Then it smiles at you. You didn't smile. "Touch the glass," it says, in your own voice. "I have something you lost."

options.label: Touch the mirror
options.outcome: The glass is ice-cold and yields like water. Something presses into your palm and you snatch your hand back. Your reflection looks satisfied. A small item rests in your hand, you have no memory of losing it.
options.chronicle: Touched a mirror whose reflection smiled when I didn't. It gave me something. I am wearing it, cautiously.

road.hint: A reflection that smiles first wants something.

options.label: Offer it some mana
options.outcome: Your reflection tilts its head and reaches through the glass to leave a rolled scroll on the floor at your feet. "A fair trade," it says. "Come back when you have more."

options.label: Walk past without looking at it
options.outcome: "Wise," your reflection says to your back. You keep walking. You are absolutely certain there was a second set of footsteps behind you. There wasn't. Probably.

name: Stone Fox
text: A fox sits in the corridor, perfectly still, watching you. Its fur is the color of granite. Its eyes are amber glass. When you stop, it stands, circles you once in complete silence, and then sits again facing away from you, clearly expecting to be followed.

options.label: Follow the fox
options.outcome: It leads you through a route you would never have chosen, winding and doubling back, and then sits before a crack in the wall. Behind it, a small chamber contains something left by a previous adventurer. The fox is gone when you turn back.
options.chronicle: Followed a fox made of stone. It led me somewhere. It did not explain.

road.hint: A fox that wants to be followed has somewhere in mind.

options.label: Offer it something to eat
options.outcome: It sniffs the offering once, then touches it with its nose and looks up at you. The amber eyes hold for a long moment. Then it breathes on you, cold and clean, and simply is no longer there. You notice you are very hard to see.

options.label: Let it sit and walk around it
options.outcome: It watches you go without moving. When you glance back from the next junction, it is already facing a different direction, as though it was never waiting for you at all.

name: Limping Lion
text: A lion lies across the passage, licking one forepaw and growling at it. The paw is swollen to twice its size around a black thorn as long as your finger. He looks at you the way a patient looks at a barber.

options.label: Take the paw in both hands and draw the thorn
options.outcome: He roars, and a claw opens your forearm before he has finished deciding not to eat you. Then the thorn is out and he is washing the paw with great dignity, as if the whole thing had been his idea. You keep the thorn. It seems like the kind of thing a person should keep.
options.chronicle: Pulled a thorn out of a lion's paw. He let me keep my arm, and I kept the thorn.

road.hint: A thorn drawn from a lion is a debt the lion remembers.

options.label: Toss him some food and edge round
options.outcome: He eats it without getting up and watches you go past with yellow eyes. The paw stays as it is.

options.label: Back away slowly
options.outcome: He lets you. The growling follows you down the passage, aimed at the paw and not at you.

name: Ysolde
text: A woman behind a fallen portcullis, her hands raw from trying to lift it, a stoppered vial tucked into her dress. "Is there anyone? My girl, Elara, she's seven, I left her with my pendant and said seven sleeps." She sees you and pushes her face to the bars. "Have you seen a little girl?"

options.label: Tell her Elara has the pendant and went home
options.outcome: Ysolde puts her forehead against the bars and laughs and cries at once. Then she braces, and you brace, and together you get the portcullis up a hand's width, then a foot. She slides under with the medicine. "Benno's fever. If I run." She runs.
options.chronicle: Told Elara's mother her girl had the pendant and had gone home. We got the gate up between us. She ran for the stair with the medicine.

road.hint: News carried up a stair is worth more than gold carried down.

options.label: Help her lift the gate
options.outcome: Together you get it up a foot and she slides under. Then she sees the pendant you carry. She looks at it for a long time. "Where is she?" You tell her. She takes the pendant out of your hand, and you let her, and she goes without another word.
options.chronicle: Helped a woman out from under a gate, and she saw her daughter's pendant on me. She took it back. I let her.

road.hint: What you kept from the child, the mother takes back.

options.label: Help her lift the gate
options.outcome: Together you get it up a foot and she slides under. "Where is she?" You tell her where you left Elara. You do not tell her about the pendant. She looks at your empty hands a long time, and then she goes.
options.chronicle: Helped Elara's mother out from under a gate and told her where I left her girl. I did not tell her about the pendant. She looked at my empty hands a long time.

road.hint: What you kept from the child, the mother reads in your empty hands.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you the portcullis grinds against her hands again.
options.chronicle: Left a woman trying to lift a portcullis with her bare hands. She was still trying when I lost the sound.

road.hint: Iron does not care how long you pull.

name: Davy Hollins
text: A boy of about sixteen lies under a fallen roof beam, pinned from the hips down, very calm in the way people are when they've decided not to panic. "Davy. Shoring boy. I told Gorran the north prop was rotten." He almost laughs. "Old Gorran says never lift a beam off a man, it kills him. Says wait for the crew." Below the beam his legs have gone a bad, waxy colour. The crew is a long way off.

options.label: Lift the beam off him now
options.outcome: It comes up with a groan of wood, and you drag him clear. The colour starts to come back into his legs, and with it the pain, and with the pain, the shock: he is going grey and cold and fast.

road.hint: Old wisdom about beams is older than the people it was meant to save.

options.label: Do as the old foreman says, and wait for the crew
options.outcome: You sit with him and wait. The crew is a long way off. By the time their lamps come round the corner, he has gone quiet, still pinned, still waiting to be lifted.
options.chronicle: Waited with Davy Hollins for his crew, because the old men say lifting a beam kills a man. The crew came. It was too late. The old men were wrong.

road.hint: Waiting is not always the careful choice.

options.label: Go for the crew yourself
options.outcome: You run for the crew and find them, and come back with them at a run, and Davy is asleep under the beam and does not wake.

options.label: Give him a healing potion
options.outcome: He drinks it in gulps. The grey goes out of his lips. "Biscuit," he says, which turns out to be his dog. He'll limp for a year. He'll live.
options.chronicle: Lifted a beam off a shoring boy named Davy and poured a potion into him before the shock took him. He will limp, and live. He told me about his dog.

options.label: Keep him flat and warm, stop the bleeding, and wait with him

pass.outcome: You lay him flat, cover him with what you can spare from your pack, raise nothing and press on the cut where the beam bit, and you talk to him so he stays with you. When the crew comes he is cold and frightened and alive.
pass.chronicle: Got a beam off Davy Hollins and kept him flat and warm and talking until his crew came. He was frightened and alive. Both, I think, are good signs.

fail.outcome: You do everything you can think of, and some of it is wrong, and the shock is quicker than you are. He goes quiet talking about his dog.
fail.chronicle: Got the beam off Davy Hollins and lost him to the shock anyway. I did not know enough. I am going to learn.

road.hint: Freeing someone is the first half of saving them.

name: The Voice in the Wall
text: The stonework here is different, older, rougher, carved with symbols that don't match the dungeon's usual aesthetic. As you examine them, a voice emanates from the stone itself, resonant and slow, like an echo that arrives before the sound. "Seeker. I have slept here longer than your civilization. I remember what was buried here first."

options.label: Ask what was here before the dungeon
options.outcome: "A city," it says. "Then a sea. Then a forest. Then silence. Then your people came and called it a dungeon, because that is the word you have for places that are old and dark and full of things you don't understand." A long pause. "You are not the strangest thing that has walked this corridor."
options.chronicle: Listened to a wall tell me what was here before the dungeon. It took a long time. Walls are patient.

road.hint: The oldest stones remember the oldest stories.

options.label: Listen to the wall's story
options.outcome: It takes a long time. Eleven thousand years compressed into an hour of stone-slow speech, civilizations that used this corridor as a parade route, as a grave, as a shortcut, as a place of worship. You ache from standing still so long, but when it finishes, it breathes out a warmth through the rock that settles on you like a blessing earned and given freely. "THANK YOU," it rumbles. "GO WELL."

options.label: Back away from the wall
options.outcome: "Wise," the wall says, without reproach. The symbols return to inert stone. The corridor feels ordinary again, or at least it feels that way until you glance back and notice the symbols have changed position.

name: Diogenes
text: A filthy old man is sitting in a large clay jar in the middle of the corridor, holding up a lit lantern although there are torches every ten paces. He shines it in your face. "I am looking for an honest man," he says. "It's been a slow century. Are you one?"

options.label: "I am."
options.outcome: He holds the lantern to your face a long time, then lowers it. "No," he says, and keeps looking past you, down the corridor.
options.chronicle: Told Diogenes I was an honest man. He held his lantern to my face a long time, and then looked past me.

road.hint: An honest man is easier to claim to be than to find.

options.label: "I am."
options.outcome: "Honest, and soft," he says. "Paid a thief's debt, didn't you? I can always tell." He keeps the lantern lit.

road.hint: An honest man is easier to claim to be than to find.

options.label: "I am."
options.outcome: He looks a long time. Then he blows the lantern out. "Then I can stop looking," he says, and sits back, satisfied. A moment later he relights it. "No. I'll check you again tomorrow."
options.chronicle: Told Diogenes I was honest. He blew out his lantern. Then he relit it, to check me again tomorrow.

road.hint: An honest man is easier to claim to be than to find.

options.label: "Not always."
options.outcome: He laughs until he coughs. "Closer than most," he says, and shares a heel of bread with you, which is most of what he has.
options.chronicle: Admitted to Diogenes I was not always honest. He laughed and gave me a heel of bread. It was most of his bread.

options.label: "Is there anything I can do for you?"
options.outcome: "Yes," he says. "Stand out of my light."
options.chronicle: Asked Diogenes if I could do anything for him. He told me to get out of his light. Alexander got the same answer.

road.hint: Some men want nothing, and that is their power.

name: Lena
text: A girl of about fourteen with her mother's satchel and her mother's squint stops square in front of you. "Mam said a stranger with a potion. Said to look for the one who didn't ask anything for it." She holds the satchel out. "You don't owe me anything. I'm here to pay."

text_variants.text: A girl of about fourteen with her mother's squint blocks the corridor, a ratting pole held like a spear. "Mam described you. Down to the boots." Her voice shakes, but the pole doesn't. "She got home. No thanks to you. I've come for her satchel."

A girl of about fourteen with her mother's satchel and her mother's squint stops square in front of you. "Mam said a stranger who knew a tourniquet. Said you swore at her leg till it listened, and didn't ask anything for it." She holds the satchel out. "You don't owe me anything. I'm here to pay."

escort_lena.name: Lena

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the stair Lena hands you the last of her mother's tonic and is back up the steps before you can argue.
on_arrive.chronicle: Lena walked me a whole floor and never once stepped on a trap. Then she went home.

on_fail.chronicle: I lost Lena on the stairs. I keep thinking about her mother's squint.

escort_lena.on_fail_trapdoor: The floor dropped out and took me without Lena. That was the floor's doing. It does not feel that way.

options.label: Take her mother's kit
options.outcome: She looks relieved, as if an account has been closed. "Mam'll be glad. She hates owing."
options.chronicle: Marta's girl found me and paid her mother's debt in potions. I took them. She seemed relieved.

road.hint: A debt paid back lets two people stop thinking about it.

options.label: "Keep it. Go home."
options.outcome: She argues. You win, narrowly. She goes back up with the satchel still on her shoulder and the look of someone who will try again.
options.chronicle: Sent Lena home with her mother's kit still on her shoulder. She argued. I won, barely.

road.hint: Refusing a repayment is a gift too, though not a free one.

options.label: "Walk me down one floor. You know the traps."
options.outcome: She grins her mother's grin. "Step where I step."

road.hint: Someone who learned the traps from her mother is worth following.

options.label: Give back what you took
options.outcome: She takes them and checks every stopper. "The jars are two short," she says. "Mam counted." She goes, and does not look back.
options.chronicle: Marta's daughter came for her mother's satchel. I gave back what I still had. She said the jars were two short. She was right.

road.hint: What you take from a mother, her daughter comes to collect.

options.label: Tell her it's all gone
options.outcome: "Then I hope it was worth it." She spits on your boots, very accurately, and goes.
options.chronicle: Told a rat-catcher's daughter her mother's medicine was spent. She spat on my boots. Good aim.

road.hint: Some accounts stay open for good.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: She watches you go, and for a moment she looks exactly like her mother.

name: Ostrander
text: A man is up to his chest in a sucking pit of black mud at the bottom of a drop. "Rope. For the love of God, a rope." His coat is a wrecker's coat, tar-black, and a dark lantern on a pole lies in the mud beside him, the kind you hang on a cliff to make ships think there is a harbour. "I know what I am," he gasps. "Pull me out anyway."

options.label: Throw him your rope
options.outcome: You haul him out. He lies on the edge coughing mud, then grins up at you with very good teeth. "You're a saint," he says. "Saints are good for business." He picks up his lantern and goes.
options.chronicle: Pulled a wrecker named Ostrander out of a mud pit. He thanked me, then took his false lantern with him.

road.hint: A rope thrown with no conditions is a gift to whatever the man does next.

options.label: Make him swear on the rope never to light a false lamp again, then pull
options.outcome: "Swear it." He looks at the rope, and at you, and at the mud at his chin. "Never another false light," he says. "On my mother's grave." You pull. He leaves the lantern in the pit.
options.chronicle: Made a wrecker swear on my rope never to light a false lamp again before I pulled him out. He left his lantern in the mud.

road.hint: A rope thrown with a condition attached can pull a man further than the pit.

options.label: Leave him
options.outcome: "I know what I am," he shouts after you. "That's why I asked."
options.chronicle: Left a wrecker in his own pit. He said he knew what he was. So did I.

road.hint: A man caught in his own trap has already told you who he is.

name: Grumwald
text: Another chasm, another rope bridge, and Grumwald, minding his cousin's bridge now, asleep beside a new box. The sign reads: TOLL ONE COPPER. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY. Underneath, in newer paint: YES, YOU.

text_variants.text: Another chasm, another rope bridge, and Grumwald, minding his cousin's bridge now, asleep beside a new box. The sign reads: TOLL ONE COPPER. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY. Underneath, in newer paint: NUMBER NINE CROSSES FREE.

Another chasm, another rope bridge, and Grumwald, minding his cousin's bridge now, asleep beside a new box. The sign reads: TOLL ONE COPPER. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY. Underneath, in newer paint: ESPECIALLY YOU. The box is chained to his ankle.

options.label: Pay the toll
options.outcome: One yellow eye opens. "Nine. Twice. That's never happened."
options.chronicle: Met Grumwald's second bridge. His sign said number nine crosses free. I paid anyway. He nearly fell off his stool.

road.hint: A troll remembers faces for a very long time.

options.label: Pay the toll
options.outcome: One yellow eye opens. "Huh," he says, and you have the feeling a long ledger has been squared, approximately.
options.chronicle: Grumwald's new sign said especially you. I paid. I think we are square, approximately.

road.hint: A troll remembers faces for a very long time.

options.label: Pay the toll
options.outcome: One yellow eye opens.

road.hint: A troll remembers faces for a very long time.

options.label: Cross
options.outcome: The bridge holds. The snoring never changes.
options.chronicle: Crossed another of Grumwald's bridges. He has added a line to his sign, and I am fairly sure it is about me.

road.hint: Every bridge you cross remembers you a little.

name: Elspeth
text: A woman with a candle in a jar is coming up the corridor against the flow of everything else, thin as a reed and walking like someone who was in bed a month ago. "Aldric said a stranger was carrying his sin for him. The cordial worked." She sets the candle down. "I've come to carry it back."

text_variants.text: A woman with a candle in a jar stops in front of you. "You're the one. The altar broke it. Aldric felt it go, all the way up in our kitchen. He sent me to say so, since he has a farm to mend."

options.label: Let her take the stone
options.outcome: She takes it in both arms and staggers, and does not complain. "There's an altar two stairs down," she says. "I'll take it there and break it, then go home light." The candle goes out. She does not relight it.
options.chronicle: Elspeth took Aldric's stone down to an altar to break it, and then home. I let her. She did not relight her candle.

road.hint: A carried burden can be handed back without being dropped.

options.label: "I gave Aldric my word. I'll finish it."
options.outcome: She looks at you a long time, then lights your way to the next stair with her candle, and goes back up alone.
options.chronicle: Elspeth offered to take the stone. I said no. It is my promise, not hers.

road.hint: Some promises are kept by refusing help.

options.label: Thank her for the news
options.outcome: She presses the candle on you, jar and all. It burns without wax, the way some candles do in old stories.
options.chronicle: Aldric's wife found me to say thank you. She left me her candle. It burns without wax.

road.hint: A candle lit for someone else's knight can show your own road too.

options.label: Keep walking
options.outcome: She watches you go, and goes on her way.

name: Man Who Is Owed
stance_note: Steel-man: Pike is sincere and selfless, and Basil the Great's sermon is the strongest Christian case for his claim, quoted accurately. The pass answers it (§3.9: a duty on the giver, not a right in the receiver) by showing the harm of the principle to a third party, not by mocking the man.
text: A gaunt man in a patched apron steps into your path with a basket. Behind him a thin girl stands silent, watching your pack. "Gerrold Pike. You carry rations; she has none. Saint Basil said it, and he meant it: the bread you hold back belongs to the hungry. It isn't yours to give. It's hers, and I'm here to collect it." He is not asking. He has the calm of a man who has never once kept back a crumb for himself.

options.label: Put a ration in his basket
options.outcome: He hands it to Nell whole, without tasting it. Then he turns to the old pilgrim coming down the stair behind you, who has one heel of bread, and holds out the basket to her as well, gently, by right. She gives it to him. She thinks she must.
options.chronicle: Paid my share to Gerrold Pike for a hungry girl. He gave her all of it. Then he collected the last crust off an old pilgrim, by right.

road.hint: A collector who means well still collects from everyone.

options.label: Give it to the girl yourself
options.outcome: Nell takes it in both hands and eats as if someone might take it back. Pike nods, satisfied but not pleased. "Good. But you'd have owed it whether you felt like giving or not."
options.chronicle: Fed a hungry girl myself rather than paying the man who said the bread was hers by right. He said I would have owed it anyway.

road.hint: A gift goes furthest from the hand that gives it.

options.label: Answer him: a gift owed is no gift at all

pass.outcome: You say it plainly. Feeding her is your duty, and you'll do it because you choose to. But Basil was telling the rich man what he ought to do, not handing anyone a warrant to collect. A gift taken by right stops being a gift and makes servants of the givers, starting with that old pilgrim. Pike is silent a long time. Then he turns, walks back up the stair to the pilgrim, and gives her bread back with both hands. "I've been taking it like a tax," he says. "Basil never asked me to be a tax."
pass.chronicle: Argued with Gerrold Pike that charity owed is no charity. He gave an old pilgrim back her bread and said Basil never asked him to be a tax.

fail.outcome: You tangle yourself up. Pike is kind about it, which is worse for the argument. He takes the ration as owed, gives it to Nell, and turns to the pilgrim.
fail.chronicle: Lost an argument about charity to a man who keeps nothing for himself. He was kind about it. The pilgrim behind me still paid.

road.hint: A duty you owe is not a debt someone else can collect.

options.label: Refuse him and walk on
options.outcome: Pike nods, unsurprised, and turns to the next traveller on the stair.
options.chronicle: Told a man collecting for the poor that my rations were mine to give. He nodded and went on to the next traveller.

road.hint: A refusal is a door shut, and the stair goes on.

name: Samson
text: A wedding feast in a cave hall, and at the head of the table a huge man with hair to his waist in seven braids. Thirty sullen young men line the benches. "Samson of Zorah. A riddle and a wager: thirty fine cloaks says you can't answer it." He grins. "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." By the door, the thirty's leader catches your sleeve. "We got it out of the bride. We said we'd burn her father's house. Pay us, and the answer's yours."

options.label: Answer it yourself, staking a fifth of your purse

pass.outcome: "A lion," you say, "and the honey the bees made in its carcass." Samson roars and slaps the table hard enough to crack it. "Honestly come by. Not like these will try to." He looks at the thirty. They look at their plates.
pass.chronicle: Answered Samson's riddle myself. A lion, and honey. He cracked the table laughing, and gave the thirty a look I would not want.

fail.outcome: You guess wrong. Samson takes your stake and shrugs, almost sorry. "Seven days, they had," he says. "You had a minute."
fail.chronicle: Lost my stake guessing at Samson's riddle. Seven days, the others had. I had a minute.

road.hint: An answer forced out of a frightened woman is not yours to sell.

options.label: Buy the answer from the thirty
options.outcome: "A lion, and honey," you say. Samson's face goes very dark. "Somebody has been talking to my bride." He pays you, and then he goes out with the thirty, and you hear what that sounds like.
options.chronicle: Bought the answer to Samson's riddle from men who had bullied it out of his bride. He paid me. Then he went to see them.

road.hint: Some answers come with the bride's tears still on them.

options.label: Tell Samson his bride was threatened, and give up the wager
options.outcome: Samson goes very quiet, which on him is terrible. He sends four of his own men to sit outside her father's house with clubs, and only then does he go looking for the thirty.
options.chronicle: Told Samson the men at his wedding had threatened to burn his bride's father's house. He sent guards first and went hunting second. Good order.

road.hint: In the old story, nobody warned him, and the house burned.

name: The Piper
text: A line of children dances down the corridor behind a tall man in a coat of red and yellow, playing a pipe. Their eyes are open and empty. Behind them a fat man in a mayor's chain runs, puffing. "Stop him. I'll pay, I'll pay." The Piper doesn't stop. "A thousand guilders, he promised, for the rats. He paid me fifty, and laughed." At the very back a small boy on a crutch is falling behind, crying to keep up.

options.label: Pay the Piper his thousand yourself
options.warning: Stop him. I'll pay, I'll pay.
options.outcome: The Piper looks at your gold, then at the mayor, then pockets it and plays a different tune. The children blink, and turn, and go home. The mayor wipes his face. "Generous," he says. "Very generous. Hamelin thanks you." He does not offer to pay you back.

delayed.text: A notice nailed to a stair-post: HAMELIN SEEKS A RAT-CATCHER. FAIR TERMS. B. HARDEKOPF, MAYOR.

options.chronicle: Paid the Piper his fee out of my own purse to bring Hamelin's children home. The mayor thanked me warmly. He is advertising for a rat-catcher again.

road.hint: Pay a cheat's debt for him and he will run up another.

options.label: Make the mayor pay what he owes, staking your breath

pass.outcome: You catch the mayor by his chain of office and hold it up so the Piper can see the town seal on it. A contract made under that seal binds Hamelin, not just Hardekopf, and Hamelin is right here, dancing. The mayor pays, in full, from the purse on his belt he swore was empty. The Piper counts it, nods, and plays the children home. The boy on the crutch is the first one back.
pass.chronicle: Held the mayor of Hamelin to his own contract in front of the Piper. He paid in full from a purse he swore was empty. The children went home.

fail.outcome: The mayor argues that the contract was for rats, not sorcery, and while you argue the music gets into your feet. You dance until you fall. When you get up, the corridor is empty except for the mayor, alone now and grey, and the boy on the crutch, who was too slow to follow, crying in the dust. The mayor takes Hans by the hand. "I'll get this one home, at least."
fail.chronicle: Argued contracts with the mayor of Hamelin while the Piper took the children into the hill. Only the lame boy was left. In the story, he always is. The mayor took him home.

road.hint: A town's seal on a promise makes the whole town the debtor.

options.label: Carry the lame boy out of the line
options.outcome: You scoop up the boy on the crutch. He fights you, crying, because he wants to go where the music is. The others go into the hill, and the hill closes. He stops fighting then. His name is Hans. The mayor, alone now and grey, takes him by the hand. "I'll get this one home, at least."
options.chronicle: Carried the lame boy out of the Piper's line. The others went into the hill. He fought me the whole way and then he stopped. The mayor took him home.

road.hint: Saving the one you can reach is still saving one.

options.label: Stand aside
options.outcome: The music goes past, and the children, and the mayor, still promising.

name: Sir Aldric
text: A knight kneels at a fresh cairn with a black stone still lashed to his back. A crystal vial lies empty beside him, the one you drank from. He does not look up, and he does not speak. A pilgrim's staff leans on the cairn; whoever brought the news down from the surface did not stay. Somebody has scratched one word on the top stone: ELSPETH.

options.label: Kneel beside him a while
options.outcome: He doesn't acknowledge you. After a long time he reaches out and straightens a stone that was already straight.
options.chronicle: Found Sir Aldric at his wife's cairn. He did not speak. I do not think he will again.

road.hint: Some answers come back as cairns.

options.label: Offer to take the stone now
options.outcome: He shakes his head once, very slowly. The stone is part of the cairn now, or he is.
options.chronicle: Offered to carry Sir Aldric's stone, far too late. He shook his head. He has decided to keep it.

road.hint: An offer made too late is still an offer, and still too late.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The stone grinds against his armour as he leans forward to rest his head on the cairn.
options.chronicle: Walked past a knight kneeling at a cairn with an empty vial beside it. I knew whose vial it was.

name: Great Lion
text: Something heavy has kept pace with you in the dark for three rooms. Now it steps into the light: a full-maned lion in his prime, scarred across the muzzle, with a pale old mark on one forepaw. He sits down in the middle of the corridor and waits to see what you'll do.

pass.outcome: You hold it low and still, palm up, eyes down, the way you'd offer something to any big cat that hasn't decided about you. He sniffs it, and then sniffs you, and then puts his whole great head against your chest and pushes, the way a house cat does.
pass.chronicle: The lion I helped came back, grown. He remembered the thorn and pushed his head against me like a house cat. Androcles had the right idea.

fail.outcome: You hold it up too fast. He flinches back, then takes the thorn delicately from your fingers in his teeth, the way a dog takes a biscuit, and walks off with it.
fail.chronicle: The lion came back. I startled him. He took the thorn and went. I think we are still on good terms.

road.hint: A kindness to a beast is repaid in the beast's own coin.

options.label: Stand very still
options.outcome: He looks at you a long time, then pads past, close enough to brush your leg.

options.label: Throw him food and back away

name: Ostrander
text: A lamp glows across a chasm, warm and inviting, as if a path ran to it. The lamp is on the wrong side of the chasm, where no path goes.

text_variants.text: At the lip of a chasm a lamp burns on an iron pole, on the right side, where the path is. A man in a wrecker's coat sits under it, trimming the wick. Ostrander. "Never another false light," he says, before you can ask. "I swore on your rope. Lamp's been lit every watch since."

options.label: Sit under his lamp a while
options.outcome: He tells you where the floor gives way.
options.chronicle: Found Ostrander keeping a true lamp at a chasm. He swore on my rope never to light a false one, and he hasn't. Some people mend.

road.hint: A lamp kept true is a promise lit again every watch.

options.label: Walk toward the light
options.outcome: The path ends a step before the light does. You fall a short, painful way into a cut where two men in wreckers' coats are waiting with clubs. Above, someone laughs and trims the wick.
options.chronicle: Walked toward a lamp across a chasm. It was Ostrander's. I pulled him out of a pit once. He has not changed his trade.

road.hint: A lamp on the wrong side of a gulf is lit for the wrong reason.

options.label: Look for whoever is holding it

pass.outcome: You find him in the shadow under the lamp, and he sees you see him. He blows it out and runs.
pass.chronicle: Caught Ostrander lighting false lamps again. He ran. I pulled him out of a pit once, which I now regret in a measured way.

fail.outcome: You see nothing but the light. You go round the long way, for no reason you can name.

road.hint: Before you follow a lamp, look for the hand holding it.

name: Lawspeaker's Rock
text: Two families face each other across a flat rock under a lamp-stone, axes held low. A big man sets a bag of silver on the rock. "Hallbjorn. I killed Kol over a whale stranded on the shore of the under-sea, and I'm sorry for it, and there's his price." Kol's brother Steinar doesn't look at the silver. "Silver doesn't eat at my table." Every face turns to you. "You're a stranger," says Hallbjorn. "Strangers have no side. Speak the law."

options.label: Speak the law: the price, the oath, the outlawry

pass.outcome: You speak it as the old lawspeakers did, case by case: the price for a free man killed in hot blood, the oath of peace sworn on the ring, the outlawry for whoever breaks it. Steinar listens to the end. Then he picks up the silver, slowly, as if it weighed more than it does, and puts out his hand.
pass.chronicle: Spoke the old law at a blood feud because the Lawspeaker was dead and I was a stranger. They took the silver instead of the axe. It nearly did not work.

fail.outcome: You stumble over the price and the oath. Steinar hears the hesitation. "Then there's no law here," he says, and the axes come up. Hallbjorn dies on the rock with his silver beside him.
fail.chronicle: Tried to speak the law at a blood feud and forgot the middle. Without the law they used axes. I keep thinking about the middle.

road.hint: Law is what stands between a grudge and an axe.

options.label: Add your own silver to sweeten the price
options.warning: Silver doesn't eat at my table.
options.outcome: Steinar looks at your coins on top of Hallbjorn's. "Now my brother's price is paid by a stranger," he says. "He's worth less than I thought." The axes come up. Hallbjorn dies on the rock, on top of both your silvers.
options.chronicle: Added my own silver to a blood price to make the peace. It made the dead man cheaper. They used axes.
