road.hint: A grieving man hears an insult in a stranger's coin.

options.label: Tell Steinar to take his revenge
options.outcome: "Blood for blood," you say, and Steinar nods as if you'd told him the weather.

delayed.text: A new cairn by the stair, two names scratched on it: Hallbjorn's sons. Under them, in a fresh hand: AND STEINAR.

options.chronicle: Told a grieving brother to take his revenge. He did. Some floors later I passed a cairn with more names on it than his.

road.hint: Blood for blood is a sum that never comes out even.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you the silence on the rock stretches, and stretches, and breaks.
options.chronicle: Walked away from a blood feud at a law rock. I heard it break behind me.

road.hint: A law rock with no lawspeaker is only a rock.

name: Talkative Old Spearman
text: A very old man in very old bronze is sitting halfway up a broken pillar, with his spear planted beside it like a ladder. "I am not stuck," he says. "I am resting where I landed. When the Boar of Calydon came at me I vaulted on this spear into a tree, and a man my age does not come down from a thing like that in a hurry. Sit. I will tell you about the hunt. All of it."

options.label: Sit down and hear all of it
options.outcome: Artemis sent the boar because a king forgot her at harvest. Half the heroes of Greece came. A huntress named Atalanta drew first blood with an arrow, which the men have not forgiven, and Meleager finished it with a spear. "They say a beast of that blood roots about below here still. Blades skid off the bristles. A point goes in." You get up stiff, and strangely ready for anything.
options.chronicle: Sat through the whole of an old spearman's story about the Calydonian Boar. It took a long time and was mostly true.

road.hint: An old soldier's story is long because he lived all of it.

options.label: Ask only where the boar is now
options.outcome: "Below. A few floors, if it is anywhere. Some years it is and some years it is not; that is boars." He looks disappointed in you. "Young people never want the middle of a story."
options.chronicle: Heard that the Calydonian Boar may be rooting about on the floors below.

options.label: Help him down and move on
options.outcome: He comes down slowly, complaining about modern pillars. "In my day," he says, "we had trees."

name: Tarek the Guard
text: A broad-shouldered man is sitting on an overturned crate, head in his hands. He looks up when he hears you, too quickly, too hopefully. "Tell me you know the way out. Or tell me you have food. Or both." He pauses. "Please, in any order."

options.label: Give him food and directions
options.outcome: He eats quickly, then stands, squaring his shoulders with visible relief. "You're a decent soul." He grips your forearm, soldier to soldier, and says a guardsman's blessing over you. "Keep your left side covered." A steadiness settles around you like a second coat.
options.chronicle: Gave a lost caravan guard food and directions. He asked in any order, so I gave both.

road.hint: Food first, then directions, then hope.

options.label: "Sorry, I'm lost myself."
options.outcome: He laughs, short, tired, genuine. "Of course you are." He nods toward the dark. "Well. Company for a few minutes, then. That's something."

name: Saint Brendan
text: In an underground sea, on a low black island with no trees, fourteen monks in wet habits are building a cookfire for an Easter supper, and an old monk in the bow of a leather boat is watching them with a look you can't read. "Brendan," he says, nodding to you. "Will you help the brothers with their fire?" The island is warm under your boots. It rises, slowly, and falls again, as if it were breathing.

options.label: Help the brothers build up the fire
options.warning: It rises, slowly, and falls again, as if it were breathing.
options.outcome: The fire catches beautifully. Then the island shudders from end to end and goes down like a stone, and you are all in black water among floating loaves and a cauldron, and Brendan is fishing monks out with a boathook, unsurprised.
options.chronicle: Helped some monks light a cookfire on an island. The island was a fish. Saint Brendan fished us out with a boathook and did not seem surprised.

road.hint: Check what you are standing on before you build a fire on it.

pass.outcome: Warm, breathing, no trees, and at the far end a hole that mists every few minutes. You get the brothers back into the boat before the fire is lit, and Brendan laughs out loud for the first time in seven years. "Then we'll say the Mass on his back without a fire," he says. "He's been patient with us." They do. You stay for it.
pass.chronicle: Spotted the island under a monk's cookfire was breathing and got them off it. They said Easter Mass on the whale's back. Saint Brendan laughed out loud.

fail.outcome: It looks like an island to you.
fail.chronicle: Looked hard at an island in an underground sea and decided it was an island. It was not.

road.hint: An island that breathes is not an island.

options.label: Share your food with the brothers
options.outcome: They bless it, and you, and then go back to building the fire.

options.label: Wish them a happy Easter and go

name: Wounded Scout
text: A young scout with a badly wrapped leg wound is propped against a pillar, pale but awake. "Don't bother with the north passage," she says immediately, as if she's been waiting to warn someone. "There's something down there that doesn't die clean." She winces and shifts her weight. "I'd offer to trade, but I'm a bit short on leverage right now."

options.label: Pay for bandages and splints (60 gold)
options.outcome: She accepts the supplies with genuine relief and presses something into your hand, a rough sketch of the northern passage, with the creature's patrol route marked in red. "It circles. There's a window of about forty seconds. That's how I got out."

options.label: Sit with her until she can walk
options.outcome: You help her re-bind the wound properly and wait while she recovers enough to stand. She insists on returning the favor, pulling out a small medkit and seeing to a few of your own injuries with a practiced hand. "Scout training," she says simply.
options.chronicle: Sat with a wounded scout until she could walk. She warned me about the north passage. I listened.

road.hint: Listen to the scout who came back.

options.label: Wish her luck and move on
options.outcome: "Yeah," she says, to no one in particular. You hope she finds her way out. You've seen enough of this dungeon to know that hope doesn't cost anything, but it isn't cheap either.

name: Bramble the Vendor
text: A heavyset halfling has set up a small cookfire in a wide junction, with something genuinely savory simmering in a pot. In a dungeon. In a pot. He stirs it cheerfully. "Before you ask: yes, I have a permit. No, I won't tell you who issued it. Yes, it smells as good as it looks. You want some or not?"

options.label: Buy a bowl (fills you up)
options.outcome: It is, genuinely, excellent. Rich, well-seasoned, served in a chipped but clean bowl. You eat it standing and feel almost civilized. "Good recipe," you manage. "Family secret," he says, and winks. "It's mushrooms. Everything down here is mushrooms."
options.chronicle: Bought stew from a halfling with a permit he would not explain. It was excellent stew.

road.hint: Do not ask who issued the permit.

options.label: Buy extra provisions
options.outcome: He packs a portion into a waxed cloth bundle with professional efficiency. "Keeps two days, three if you don't think about it too hard." He tucks a small herb packet in with it. "For flavor. Even emergencies deserve flavor."

options.label: "Just enjoying the smell."
options.outcome: "Free of charge," he says magnanimously. You stand there for a moment longer than strictly necessary, and he doesn't rush you. Some kindnesses are very small and very important.

name: Brunhild Irontemper
text: A stout dwarven woman sits beside a portable forge, hammering sparks off a blade that glows faint orange. She squints up at you through a curtain of soot-black hair. "Weapon's looking a bit sad, isn't it? I can fix that, for a fair price."

options.label: Pay her to sharpen your weapon
options.outcome: Brunhild works with practiced efficiency, her hammer ringing in short, precise strokes. When she hands the weapon back, it catches the torchlight differently, sharper, hungrier. "Now that's a proper tool," she mutters approvingly.
options.chronicle: Paid a dwarven smith named Brunhild to fix my weapon. She called it sad. It is less sad now.

road.hint: A smith who insults your blade is about to improve it.

options.label: "Just browsing, thanks."
options.outcome: She shrugs and returns to her work without ceremony. The rhythmic clanging follows you down the corridor long after she disappears from sight.

name: Old Veska
text: An elderly woman rummages through a pile of broken weapons with the methodical joy of someone with a lifelong hobby. She holds up a snapped sword hilt to the light with genuine admiration. "Fine craftsmanship, even ruined." She notices you. "Ah! You've got equipment that still works. Interesting."

options.label: Trade gold for her oddments
options.outcome: She rummages through her bag and produces a trinket that looks like scrap but hums faintly at the correct frequency. "Found that one near a collapsed shrine. Something still lives in it." She seems delighted by your uncertainty.
options.chronicle: Traded with an old woman who loves broken weapons. She looked at mine with professional pity.

road.hint: Broken things still tell you how well they were made.

options.label: Let her examine your weapon
options.outcome: She handles your weapon with the reverence of a surgeon and the familiarity of a smith. "Made by a left-handed craftsman, mid-period, before the iron shortages, see the taper? The original owner survived at least three major campaigns." She hands it back. "You're the latest chapter. Try to be a good one."

options.label: Decline and keep moving
options.outcome: "Sensible," she says, already turning back to her pile. "Most things worth finding are worth finding by accident anyway."

name: Apprentice Runescribe
text: A teenager in oversized apprentice robes is carefully inscribing runes onto the dungeon floor and muttering to herself. She looks up with the startled expression of someone who forgot monsters also use this hallway. "Oh! Oh good, you look human. You don't happen to know what the seventh ward-rune of Kessari looks like, do you?"

options.label: Help her with the rune (costs focus)
options.outcome: You guide her hand through the symbol from memory, or perhaps intuition. It clicks into place with a soft blue flash. "That's it! Yes!" She beams and rummages in her bag. "Here, Master's reference scroll, copied it myself. You earned it."
options.chronicle: Helped a nervous apprentice finish a rune. It did not explode, which she said was unusual.

road.hint: A rune half drawn is a rune half dangerous.

options.label: Buy one of her scrolls (55 gold)
options.outcome: A fair exchange. She drives a harder bargain than her age suggests, but the scroll she produces is clearly from a higher-level compendium than anything she should have access to. You decide not to ask how she got it.

options.label: "I don't know runes. Good luck."
options.outcome: "Right. Okay. I'll figure it out." She turns back to her work with the particular determination of someone who has been underestimated their whole life and has stopped minding.

name: Thökk

tells: the white seams of old stitches
a salmon tail in her pot
laughs like someone who has just knocked over a lamp

text: In a cave mouth sits an old giantess in rags by a cookfire, with a salmon tail sticking out of her pot. Outside, everything is weeping: water runs down the stones in sheets, and a tired young god with a messenger's staff is waiting at the cave mouth. "Hermod," he says. "Ask her. She'll not weep for my brother." The old woman laughs like someone who has just knocked over a lamp. Her lips have the white seams of old stitches. "Thökk will weep dry tears," she says. "Let Hel keep what she has." She holds out a red-gold ring to you. "And you'll say nothing."

options.label: Take her ring and say nothing
options.outcome: She closes your fingers round it. Outside, Hermod waits a long time, and then goes home alone.
options.chronicle: Took a ring from an old giantess who would not weep for a dead god, and said nothing. His brother went home alone.

road.hint: A gift for silence is payment for something.

options.label: Refuse her ring, look hard at her mouth, and tell Hermod what you see

pass.outcome: "Those are Brokk's stitches," you say. "The dwarf who sewed Loki's mouth." Hermod's face goes very still. The old woman laughs one last time and is not there: a fly goes out of the cave, very fast. Baldr will stay in Hel. But now the gods know who kept him there, and Loki will answer for it with a long binding.
pass.chronicle: Recognised the stitches on an old giantess's mouth and told Hermod. She turned into a fly. Baldr stays dead. Now they know who to blame.

fail.outcome: You know you have seen those scars somewhere, and you cannot say where. Hermod thanks you anyway and goes home with nothing but the knowledge that one creature in the world would not weep.
fail.chronicle: Refused a ring from an old woman who would not weep for Baldr. I knew her face from somewhere. I still cannot place it.

road.hint: The only creature that would not weep had a reason not to.

options.label: Weep for Baldr yourself
options.outcome: You do. It is not hard; everything around you is weeping. It changes nothing. "Dry tears," says Thökk, pleased.
options.chronicle: Wept for a god called Baldr because the whole world was weeping for him. It was easy, and it did not help.

road.hint: Every voice in the world but one is still not every voice.

name: Aristodemus
text: A Spartan in a red cloak gone brown sits polishing a bronze shield that is already polished. "Aristodemus. You'll have heard. Sent home sick from the Hot Gates while the three hundred died. They call me the Trembler. Nobody speaks to me. Nobody gives me fire." He tests the spear-point with his thumb. "There's a horde below. I mean to die in front of it so well they'll have to stop calling me that. Tell me I'm right."

text_variants.text: A Spartan in a red cloak gone brown sits polishing a bronze shield that is already polished. "Aristodemus. You'll have heard. Sent home sick from the Hot Gates while the three hundred died. They call me the Trembler. Nobody speaks to me. Nobody gives me fire." He tests the spear-point with his thumb. "There's a horde below. I mean to die in front of it so well they'll have to stop calling me that. Tell me I'm right." He frowns. 'A Legion boy came through here telling my story to himself. Got the ending wrong, I hope.'

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the stair he stops. 'You walk like someone who means to go home,' he says. 'I'd forgotten that was allowed.' He goes back up, toward the light.
on_arrive.chronicle: Walked a floor with the Trembler. At the stair he said I walked like someone who meant to go home, and went home himself.

on_fail.chronicle: The Trembler fell beside me on the stair, facing the right way. Nobody can call him that now. I wish he had not had to prove it.

options.label: "Live. Dying well won't change what they call you."
options.outcome: He looks at you as if you'd slapped him, and then, slowly, as if you hadn't.

delayed.text: A bronze vault door on the stair has been forced and wedged open with a Spartan spear. The hoarder inside will not be needing his things.

options.chronicle: Told the Trembler to live. He did not like it. A few floors down I found a vault door wedged open with a Spartan spear.

road.hint: A man told to live may still find a use for his spear.

options.label: "Go and die well."
options.outcome: He stands, and the cloak hangs right on him for the first time.

delayed.text: A low doorway on the stair has a bronze shield wedged across it, face out, polished, with a spear-point broken off in the rim. Behind it, a caravan's children are asleep in a heap of blankets, unharmed. Of the Spartan there is no sign.

options.chronicle: Told the Trembler to go and die well. A few floors down I found his shield wedged across a doorway with children asleep behind it.

road.hint: A shield is a door for the people behind it.

options.label: "Walk a floor with me first, and decide on the way."
options.outcome: "A floor," he says. "One."

road.hint: A floor walked beside someone can change which way he goes next.

options.label: Call him what they call him
options.outcome: "Trembler," you say. He nods as if you had told him the time, and goes back to his shield.
options.chronicle: Called a Spartan the Trembler to his face. He just nodded. I think he has heard it from better people than me.

road.hint: A name thrown at a man who already carries it only adds weight.

name: Doctor Finch
text: A figure in a long black coat and a beaked mask stands in a doorway, clipboard in hand. "Ah. A living one." Their voice is nasal and clinical through the mask. "I've been cataloguing the afflictions down here. You look relatively intact, remarkable, given the level. Any symptoms I should note? Bleeding, visions, involuntary cursing?"

options.label: Submit to a quick examination
options.outcome: They prod and poke with cool efficiency, muttering notes. "Minor lacerations, dehydration, one infected bite you clearly hadn't noticed. Hold still." The treatment is brisk and uncomfortable, but the results are undeniable. You feel substantially better than you did walking in.
options.chronicle: Let a beaked doctor examine me. He seemed disappointed I was so healthy.

road.hint: A doctor who catalogues the dead wants a living one for once.

options.label: Buy a curative compound
options.outcome: They produce a small vial from a rack of identical vials and label it in tiny, precise handwriting. "Take with water. Do not take with alcohol. Do not take with other potions unless you understand what you're doing, which you probably don't." Charming bedside manner.

options.label: "I'm fine. Good day, Doctor."
options.outcome: "You are demonstrably not fine," they say, and make a note on their clipboard anyway. You find this oddly comforting.

name: Morrow
text: A man in a stolen priest's cassock waits on the stair with two friends in locust masks. Morrow spreads his hands, smiling. "You freed me. I've brought friends to say thank you."

text_variants.text: A man in a stolen priest's cassock waits on the stair with two friends in locust masks. Morrow spreads his hands, smiling. "You freed me. I've brought friends to say thank you." 'The old man told you I'd be back, didn't he? He always did ruin a surprise.'

options.label: Fight
options.outcome: They come at you on the stair. Morrow fights in the cassock to the end, which tells you something about him.
options.chronicle: The cultist I freed came back with friends to thank me. We settled it on the stairs. The robe did not suit him.

road.hint: Mercy to the wrong man is repaid on a stair, with interest.

options.label: Remind him you saved his life
options.outcome: "You did," Morrow says. "That's why I'm letting you go first."
options.chronicle: Told the cultist I freed that he owed me his life. He agreed, and attacked me anyway. Gratitude is not a cult virtue.

road.hint: A debt owed by a liar is not a debt.

name: Calla Strand
text: A battle-scarred woman sits with her back to the wall, methodically oiling a short sword she clearly does not intend to use again tonight. There are too many fresh bandages on her arms. "You've got that look," she says without glancing up. "Like you're still believing this was a good idea."

options.label: Ask her for combat advice
options.outcome: She talks for a while about footwork and threat angles and reading monster tells, the kind of advice that sounds boring until you're surrounded. Something about it settles into your muscles rather than your mind. Your movements feel a fraction sharper, a fraction faster.

options.label: Ask her for a sparring lesson (costs SP)
options.outcome: She raises an eyebrow but nods. She spends an hour drilling you in proper defensive stances and controlled breathing under pressure.
options.chronicle: Sparred with a retired pit fighter named Calla Strand. She hit me in the same rib three times to make a point. Point taken.

road.hint: A fighter who has stopped counting has started living.

options.label: "Just passing through."
options.outcome: "Sure you are," she says, with the tone of someone who has heard that line from people who didn't make it. She goes back to oiling her sword. You go back to believing.

name: Exposed Child
stance_note: Steel-man: Hrolf's relativism is given its strongest form (your people burn witches; every people judges by its own law; exposure as mercy in a famine). The pass text keys the reformer's dilemma (§3.10). No option rewards "whatever a hall approves is right".
text: Outside a longhouse built into the rock, a newborn lies wrapped in a fleece on a cold stone, crying thinly. Her foot is twisted. The chief stands over her with his arms folded. "Hrolf Ketilsson. A hard winter, and a lame mouth. In our hall this is right." He meets your eye. "Your people burn witches and call that right. Mine leave a weak child to the gods; it's kinder than a winter of starving. Every people judges by its own law. Who are you to judge mine?"

pass.outcome: You ask him about the first chief of his people who ever made the law kinder: was that man wrong, because the hall had not yet approved? And the first one who refused to set a child on the stone? If his hall is always right, no hall can ever become better than it was, only different. Hrolf is quiet a long time. Then his wife comes out and picks up the baby, and he does not stop her.
pass.chronicle: Asked a hall-chief whether the first of his people to make the law kinder had been wrong. He had no answer. His wife picked up the baby.

delayed.text: A Brother in a patched brown habit from the house on the side stair catches you up. "Hrolf's wife brought the little one to us for the winter, where the hall can't change its mind. She feeds like a wolf cub. We named her Astrid."
delayed.chronicle: A Brother from the side stair found me. Hrolf's wife brought the girl from the stone to them for the winter. She is feeding. They named her Astrid.

fail.outcome: He has an answer for everything you say. So you pick the baby up yourself, fleece and all, and carry her to the Brothers' house on the side stair, and he lets you, because by his law she is nobody's now.
fail.chronicle: Lost an argument with a hall-chief about leaving babies on stones, so I took the baby. By his law she belonged to nobody. By mine she did.

delayed.text: A Brother in a patched brown habit from the house on the side stair catches you up. "The girl you carried in is feeding. Her mother comes at night, when the hall is asleep. We named her Astrid."
delayed.chronicle: A Brother from the side stair found me. The girl I carried in from the stone is feeding, and her mother comes at night. They named her Astrid.

road.hint: Every custom you would defend was once somebody's new idea.

options.label: Buy the child for the price of her winter's keep
options.outcome: He takes the money and does not argue. Then his wife comes out of the longhouse and lifts the baby off the stone, because the coin is her winter's bread now, and she goes back in without a word to either of you. The custom stands. The next one will be on the stone too.
options.chronicle: Paid a hall-chief the price of a winter's bread for a baby he was leaving on a stone. His wife took her back inside. The next baby will be on the stone too.

road.hint: Buying one child off a custom keeps the custom open for business.

delayed.text: A Brother in a patched brown habit from the house on the side stair catches you up. "Hrolf's wife brought her girl to us to be blessed, the one your gold bought back. She is feeding. They named her Astrid."
delayed.chronicle: A Brother from the side stair found me. The girl my gold bought off the stone is feeding. Her mother named her Astrid.

options.label: Walk on. His hall, his law
options.outcome: The crying follows you a long way down the corridor. Then it doesn't.
options.chronicle: Walked past a baby on a stone because it was their custom. The crying stopped before I reached the stair.

road.hint: Their law, their hall, and a crying that stopped.

name: Scholar Evaine
text: A woman in ink-stained robes sits cross-legged in the middle of the corridor, surrounded by open tomes and hasty notes. She doesn't look up when you approach. "Fascinating, the rune patterns here indicate this section was built at least four centuries before the outer chambers. Oh. You're a person. Hello."

options.label: Ask about the dungeon's history
options.outcome: She launches into an enthusiastic lecture about ley-line intersections and builder-cult symbology. Most of it washes over you, but something about the way she describes spatial awareness clarifies your own perception of the space around you. Your senses sharpen unexpectedly.
options.chronicle: Heard a scholar explain the dungeon is older than the city above it. She did not look up once.

road.hint: The stones down here were cut before the city was dreamed of.

options.label: Buy a scroll from her notes
options.outcome: She tears a page from a secondary notebook with minimal hesitation. "Copied that one twice anyway." The transcription is meticulous, the ink still faintly warm from her pen.

options.label: "I'll leave you to your research."
options.outcome: "Mm. Wise choice, I'm nearly at a breakthrough." She's already forgotten you, her quill scratching furiously at a new page.

name: Gyges
text: A shepherd sits at the lip of a chasm, turning a gold ring on his finger. Each time he turns it he flickers out and back. Far below in the chasm, a bronze horse lies on its side with its belly open. "It was on a dead giant's hand, down there," he says. "Since I put it on I've taken a purse, a goat, and a girl's silver comb, and nobody saw." He pulls it off and holds it out. "Take it, or put it back on him. I can't do either." His hand keeps going to the empty finger.

options.label: Take the ring and keep it
options.outcome: He lets it go with a sound like a sob and a laugh at once. "Better you than me," he says, and then, already doubtful: "Is it?"
options.chronicle: Was given the Ring of Gyges by a shepherd who could not stop using it. He said better me than him. Then he asked whether it was.

road.hint: A ring that hides you from everyone hides you from yourself first.

options.label: Climb down and put it back on the dead giant's hand
options.outcome: The climb is long and the bronze is cold. The giant's hand is the size of a cart. You push the ring back on, and for a moment you are very tempted to turn it once, just to see. You don't. Up top, the shepherd is crying with relief.
options.chronicle: Climbed down a chasm to put the Ring of Gyges back on a dead giant's finger. I was tempted to turn it once, just to see. I did not.

road.hint: The hardest thing to put back is the thing that makes you unseen.

options.label: Promise to hold it for him until he's ready
options.warning: His hand keeps going to the empty finger.
options.outcome: He thanks you and sits beside you while you check your pack. Nobody sees anything at all. When you look up, the ring is gone, and so is a share of your purse, and so is he.
options.chronicle: Offered to keep a magic ring safe for a shepherd until he was ready to give it up. I looked away for a moment and nobody saw anything. My purse is lighter.

road.hint: A man cannot lend you the thing he cannot let go of.

name: Boundary Stone
text: A boundary stone on a moor of grey moss, with six holes bored in it and filled with vinegar. Coins lie in the vinegar. Beyond it a village has shut itself in against the plague, on its rector's word. A man in the doorway of the nearest cottage calls to you. "I'm well. I swear before God I'm well. My children are at Low Middleton, a few stairs down. Lift the bar." He keeps his collar buttoned to the chin, though the cave is close and warm, and his face shines with sweat while he shivers.

options.label: Lift the bar and let him go
options.warning: He keeps his collar buttoned to the chin, though the cave is close and warm
options.outcome: He shakes your hand hard, both of his around yours, and goes for the stair at a run.

delayed.text: At the foot of the stair a bell is tolling in Low Middleton. It tolls every hour you are on this floor.

options.chronicle: Let a man out of a plague village because he swore he was well. He shook my hand with both of his. A bell has been tolling ever since.

road.hint: A buttoned collar in a warm cave is hiding something.

options.label: Look at him properly before you lift anything

pass.outcome: You ask him to open his collar, and he knows why, and he does it anyway. A swelling the size of a pigeon's egg under his jaw, hot to the touch, and his skin is burning with fever though he shivers. He sits down on his side of the stone and cries. You sit down on yours. You stay until his lamp burns low, and promise to leave word at the stone for his children. He writes a letter for Low Middleton and drops it in the vinegar, and you fish it out and leave it under the stone where the carriers look.
pass.chronicle: Saw the plague swelling under a man's jaw before I let him out. We sat either side of the boundary stone a long while. I left his letter under it for the carriers.

fail.outcome: You look, and see a frightened man with his collar done up.
fail.chronicle: Looked at a man from a plague village and saw only a frightened father. I lifted the bar. I have regretted few things more.

road.hint: Before you open a sealed gate, ask why it was sealed.

options.label: Leave coins in the vinegar for their supplies
options.outcome: The coins sink into the vinegar. When the watch changes, the village will find them and buy bread with them, and the baker will wash them twice. Hawksworth watches you from the doorway, and does not ask again.
options.chronicle: Left coins in the vinegar at a plague village's boundary stone. They will buy bread with them, and wash them first.

road.hint: Some help is best passed over a boundary, not through it.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Please," he says, once, and then nothing.

name: Brother Osias
text: A monk with a shaved head and eyes closed in meditation sits absolutely still in the corridor, hands folded in his lap. He speaks without opening his eyes. "You carry exhaustion like a second pack. I can ease it, but concentration requires an anchor, something to focus the breath."

options.label: Let him guide a meditation session
options.outcome: He leads you through a breathing exercise that feels simple and somehow bottomless. You follow his voice into a quiet space inside yourself you had forgotten existed. When you return, your mind feels clean and your magical reserves have replenished themselves.
options.chronicle: Let a monk guide my breathing for a while. My head is quieter.

road.hint: A quiet mind carries further than a full pack.

options.label: Offer food to support his vigil
options.outcome: He opens his eyes for the first time and accepts the food with a slight bow. "Sustaining the body sustains the spirit." He shares a brief blessing that warms your muscles from the inside, like a long-forgotten memory of sunshine.

options.label: Pass quietly without disturbing him
options.outcome: He does not acknowledge your passage. But as you round the bend, you could swear the silence behind you is a fraction more peaceful than the silence ahead.

name: Courteous Giant
text: A giant sits at a table far too long for the room it is in, and the room does not seem to mind. "Nobody stays in my hall who cannot do one thing well," he says pleasantly. "We keep it modest. Empty my drinking horn. Lift my cat off the floor. Or wrestle my old nurse, Elli, if you can wake her." The horn is long, the cat is grey and very large, and the nurse is asleep by the fire.

pass.outcome: You drink until your eyes water and the level drops the width of a finger. The giant goes rather pale. "The far end of that horn lies in the sea. You have lowered it. People will call that the tide."
pass.chronicle: Drank from a giant's horn in Utgard and lowered the sea a little.

fail.outcome: You drink and drink and the horn stays full. "Thor did no better," says the giant kindly, "and he was a god."
fail.chronicle: Lost a drinking contest to a horn. In my defence, the far end was in the sea.

road.hint: In a giant's hall, the contest is never quite what it looks like.

options.label: Get both arms under the cat and lift

pass.outcome: One grey paw leaves the ground. "That cat is the serpent that circles the world. Nobody was supposed to move it at all."
pass.chronicle: Lifted one paw of a giant's cat. It was not a cat.

fail.outcome: The cat arches and does not leave the floor. It yawns at you.
fail.chronicle: Failed to lift a giant's cat. It yawned. It was, I learned later, a world serpent, which helps a little.

road.hint: In a giant's hall, the contest is never quite what it looks like.

options.label: Wake the old nurse and wrestle her

pass.outcome: She puts you down on one knee, gently, like a parcel. "Elli is Old Age. Nobody beats her. Most do not last as long as you did."
pass.chronicle: Wrestled an old woman named Elli and lost. Everyone does. I lasted longer than most.

fail.outcome: She puts you down at once. "Elli is Old Age," says the giant. "You'll meet her again."
fail.chronicle: Wrestled Old Age and lost very quickly. I am told everyone does in the end.

road.hint: In a giant's hall, the contest is never quite what it looks like.

options.label: Decline his contests
options.outcome: "Then you cannot stay," says the giant, pleasantly. "But you may certainly go." The door is a long way off, and the grey cat watches you all the way to it.
options.chronicle: Turned down a giant's three contests in his hall of tricks. He let me go. His cat watched me all the way to the door.

road.hint: A contest you decline cannot fool you.

name: The Hermit
text: Huddled against a wall in a chamber that smells of old smoke and dried herbs, a figure wrapped in layers of mismatched cloth watches you with sharp, intelligent eyes. "I've lived down here twelve years," they say softly. "I know its moods. Its secrets. You look like someone who could use a secret."

options.label: Trade stamina for their knowledge
options.outcome: They take your hands and press them flat against the stone wall. "Listen," they whisper. "Really listen." You stand there until your legs ache, and then you hear it: the subtle grammar of the dungeon, the spaces between its walls. Your awareness of the surrounding area expands like a held breath released.

options.label: Share a meal together
options.outcome: You sit together in comfortable silence, sharing food like two people who have long since run out of small talk. When you rise to leave, you feel more settled than you have in days. Sometimes stillness is its own kind of strength.
options.chronicle: Shared a meal with a hermit who has lived down here twelve years. They knew the floor's moods.

road.hint: Twelve years in the dark teaches the dark's moods.

options.label: "I prefer my own counsel."
options.outcome: They nod slowly, with no offense taken. "That's how I started too," they say. You're not entirely sure what they mean by that.

name: Mimir's Well
text: A well of black water in a root-hung cave, and in the water, just below the surface, a man's head with its eyes open, a beard spread out like weed. At the very bottom, very small, something white catches the light, round as a coin, looking up. The head speaks without bubbles. "Mimir. I keep the well. Wisdom costs. Everyone asks how much."

text_variants.text: A well of black water in a root-hung cave, and in the water, just below the surface, a man's head with its eyes open, a beard spread out like weed. At the very bottom, very small, something white catches the light, round as a coin, looking up. The head speaks without bubbles. "Mimir. I keep the well. Wisdom costs. Everyone asks how much." The head smiles. 'He sent you. He always sends the clever ones. Tell him the eye is keeping well.'

options.label: Drink, and pay what it costs
options.outcome: The water is so cold it hurts your teeth, and then your head, and then it doesn't hurt at all, and for a moment you understand something very large, and know a question no giant can answer. It goes. Some of it stays.
options.chronicle: Drank from Mimir's well. It cost me something. I understood the whole world for a moment and then most of it left. Some of it is still here.

road.hint: Wisdom from a well is paid for before you drink, not after.

options.label: "What's that at the bottom?"
options.outcome: "An eye," says Mimir. "A god paid it for one drink. He thought it cheap. He's usually right about prices."

name: Sword in the Anvil
text: A churchyard under the rock, a great stone with an anvil on it, and gold letters: WHOSO PULLETH OUT THIS SWORD OF THIS STONE AND ANVIL IS RIGHTWISE KING BORN. The anvil is empty. A big young knight holds the sword aloft. "Sir Kay. I drew it." Behind him a skinny squire stares at his own hands. The squire's hands are red from the hilt; Kay's are clean. Kay leans close. "Say you saw me draw it. Tell my father so, and you'll eat at my table all your days."

options.label: Back Kay's claim
options.outcome: Sir Ector looks at Kay, and at you, and at the skinny boy. "Is it so?" You say it is. The boy says nothing, because nobody has ever asked him anything.
options.chronicle: Swore to Sir Ector that Kay drew the sword from the anvil. It was the skinny squire. I am to eat at Kay's table all my days.

road.hint: A false witness is paid at the table and charged at the gate.

options.label: Tell Sir Ector what you saw
options.outcome: Ector goes very quiet. Then he kneels, an old man in a churchyard, to the boy he raised. Kay goes red, then white, and then, give him his due, kneels too.
options.chronicle: Turned down a knight's table for life to tell his father who really drew the sword. It was the squire. The old man knelt to him.

road.hint: The truth about who drew the sword is worth more than a seat at any table.

options.label: Put it back in the anvil and let them both try

pass.outcome: You remember how the old test went. Kay strains until his face is purple, and when he gives up he takes it out on your ribs. The squire draws it like a knife from butter, twice, looking more frightened each time. Sir Ector kneels.
pass.chronicle: Made Sir Kay put the sword back in the anvil and try again. He could not. His little brother could, twice. The old man knelt.

fail.outcome: Kay snatches it back before you can explain the test. "We're done here," he says, and you are.
fail.chronicle: Tried to set Kay and his squire the old test of the anvil, and Kay would not stand for it. At least I did not lie for him.

road.hint: A true sword can be put back and drawn again. A lie cannot.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Good," says Kay. "Friend." Behind you, an old man's voice: "Kay? Who drew it?"

name: Damocles
text: A long table laid for a king under a crystal ceiling, and at its head a gold couch, and on the couch a courtier in a crown, very pale, not eating. "I said kings were lucky," he tells you, without moving his head. "I would like to take it back now." Above him, point down, on a single horsehair, hangs a sword. The horsehair runs up to a hook, and from the hook a thin cord runs to a bell above the guards' door. A tired, clever man at the table's foot waves at you. "Dionysius. My friend Damocles envied kings. Take his place, if you like, and eat like one."

options.label: Cut the horsehair down and pull him clear
options.warning: from the hook a thin cord runs to a bell above the guards' door.
options.outcome: The hair parts, the sword falls into the soup, and the bell above the door rings like the end of the world. Damocles is clear. The guards come through the door, and they are not interested in the lesson.
options.chronicle: Cut the horsehair over Damocles and pulled him clear. The cord rang a bell. The guards did not care about the lesson. Damocles hid under the table.

road.hint: A thread that holds a sword may hold a bell as well.

options.label: Tell Dionysius the lesson has been learned, and show him you know it too

pass.outcome: You tell him what the sword is for: so his guest feels what the king feels at every meal, which is the whole of the lesson, and Damocles has felt it for three courses. A tyrant who goes on teaching it after it is learned is only showing how much he enjoys the sword. Dionysius looks at you for a long moment, then laughs, and nods to Damocles. "Get up, then." Damocles gets up very carefully, and sits down on the floor, and cries.
pass.chronicle: Talked a tyrant into letting Damocles off his couch by telling him the lesson was already learned. Damocles sat on the floor and cried.

fail.outcome: You explain the lesson back to him, and get the point of it wrong, and Dionysius smiles in a way you do not like. "Then perhaps you should sit there and learn it."
fail.chronicle: Tried to explain the sword of Damocles to the tyrant who hung it. He sat me under it until I understood. I understand.

road.hint: The lesson of the sword is short. Only a tyrant keeps teaching it.

options.label: Take his place for an hour, and eat like a king

pass.outcome: Damocles gets up and nearly falls over thanking you. You eat like a king and never once stop watching the hair, and you get up before you can forget to.
pass.chronicle: Took Damocles's place under the sword and ate a king's dinner, watching the hair the whole time. I left before dessert.

fail.outcome: You relax. The hair doesn't. You throw yourself sideways as it falls and it opens your shoulder instead of your skull. Damocles is free, at least.
fail.chronicle: Took Damocles's place under the sword and forgot about it for one moment. My shoulder remembers it for me.

road.hint: The feast is the same. It is the sword that tells you what a crown costs.

options.label: Leave him there
options.outcome: Dionysius shrugs. "He'll be there at breakfast." Damocles does not look away from the hair.
options.chronicle: Left Damocles on his couch under the sword. The king said he would still be there at breakfast. I believe him.

name: The Witch-Finder
text: A mill pond, a crowd with pitchforks, and a woman tied thumb to toe on the bank. A man in a tall black hat reads from a paper. "Matthew Hopkins. At Manningtree a witch killed a child with a look and nobody did anything. I did something." He nods at the woman. "If she sinks she's innocent. If she floats, God's water has refused her." He mentions, as a man mentions the weather, that the town pays him twenty shillings a witch. The crowd behind him has pitchforks and is very large. Alys looks at you. "I set their bones," she says. "That's all."

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Hopkins does not look up from his paper. Behind you the crowd begins to count, slowly, and somewhere past twelve it goes quiet.
options.chronicle: Walked away from a witch-finder's ducking. Behind me the crowd counted, and then went quiet. I did not turn round.

road.hint: A crowd that has made up its mind does not need you to watch.

options.label: Cut her loose and run with her
options.outcome: You get her free and three steps up the bank before the crowd closes. You come out of it bloody, with Alys over your shoulder, and the whole village now sure of two witches instead of one. At the stair she slides down and runs. "I know the back ways. You'd only slow me."
options.chronicle: Cut an herbalist loose from the witch-finder's ducking and ran. The whole village came after us. Now they think there are two witches. They may be onto something.

road.hint: A crowd convinced by a trick is not unconvinced by a sword.

options.label: Take his test apart in front of the crowd, staking your own name

pass.outcome: You ask the miller what floats. Wood, he says. And ducks, says a boy. And a woman tied in a ball with air in her lungs, you say, any woman, and you offer to tie Hopkins the same way and see. Somebody laughs. Then a lot of people do. Hopkins leaves with his paper and his hat, quickly, and Alys gives you a kit of her cures with shaking hands.
pass.chronicle: Showed a crowd that anyone tied in a ball floats, and offered to swim the witch-finder to prove it. He left quickly. The herbalist gave me her cures.

fail.outcome: You get tangled in it, and Hopkins is quicker. "Mark how the witch's friend speaks for her," he says, and the crowd turns.
fail.chronicle: Tried to argue a witch-finder down in front of a crowd and lost them. They swam her. Then they came for me.

road.hint: A test that every innocent fails is not a test.

options.label: Pay Hopkins his fee to let her go
options.warning: the town pays him twenty shillings a witch.
options.outcome: He takes your gold with a little bow and cuts her bonds himself. "The Lord is merciful, and so am I, for a consideration." Alys runs.

delayed.text: A broadsheet nailed to a stair-post: WITCH-FINDER GENERAL SWIMS TWO AT HOLLOWAY MILL. FEES AS USUAL.

options.chronicle: Paid a witch-finder his fee to let an herbalist go. He bowed and let her go. A few floors on, I read he had swum two more the next week.

road.hint: Pay a man for a kindness and he will sell the next one too.

name: The Moth Woman
text: A woman stands perfectly still in the center of the room, arms slightly extended, skin dusted with iridescent powder that catches the torchlight like wings. Her eyes are entirely silver. "You are drawn here the way all things are drawn to light," she says. "Let me look at you. I will tell you what I see."

options.label: Let her read you (costs mana)
options.outcome: She circles you slowly, trailing a finger through the air near your face, reading something invisible. When she stops, she presses one dusty fingertip to your temple. "There. I have opened a window." The world snaps into sharper focus, colors brighter, distances clearer. You perceive more than you did before.
options.chronicle: Let a woman with silver eyes read me. She knew things. I did not ask how.

road.hint: Things drawn to a flame are not always moths.

options.label: Ask what she is
options.outcome: "A question with an answer you do not have a frame for yet." She tilts her head, and the silver eyes catch the light at a new angle. "Ask me again when you have seen the deeper dark. You will understand better then."

options.label: Back away from her
options.outcome: She does not follow. She watches you retreat with those silver eyes and does not blink once. Around the corner, you check your reflection in your blade. Your own eyes look briefly, impossibly, silver. Then they don't.

name: The Shade
text: Something that might be a shadow, but isn't, peels itself from the wall. It has the rough shape of a person and the approximate manners of one. "I collect things that people don't know they're carrying," it says, in a voice that seems to come from slightly behind where it's standing. "Are you interested in a transaction?"

options.label: Offer stamina for invisibility
options.outcome: It reaches forward and takes something from you that you cannot name, a weight you hadn't noticed until its absence. In exchange, it drapes something else over you: a quality of unseeing, of negative presence. For a time, the dungeon will look through you.
options.chronicle: Traded some of my stamina to a shadow for a little invisibility. It said I would not miss it. I miss it.

road.hint: A shadow collects what you did not know you were carrying.

options.label: Ask what it collects exactly
options.outcome: "Small things. Regrets about turns not taken. Certainties that have gone stale. The memory of a face you've almost lost." It seems to consider. "I do not take anything important. Only what has already begun to cost more than it's worth."

options.label: Refuse and walk away
options.outcome: "As you wish." It does not move to stop you. It simply returns to the wall, and the wall accepts it without argument. You do not look back, but you are certain, completely certain, that nothing follows you.

name: Watch Sergeant
text: Four soldiers of the City Watch hold a barricade of overturned tables, a long way below any city. The sergeant has the look of a woman who was told to wait for orders and waited. "We were promised a courier," she says. "Iron scroll case, Watch seal. Without it we don't know which gate to fall back on, and nor do the companies above."

options.label: Hand over Edric's dispatch
options.outcome: She breaks the seal, reads it once, and starts giving orders before she has finished reading. Two runners go up the stairs at a sprint. "He didn't make it, then," she says. You tell her he made it almost all the way. She writes that down. Somewhere far overhead, a city has a better night than it was going to have.
options.chronicle: Delivered Edric's dispatch to Sergeant Holt. I told her he made it almost all the way. She wrote it down in the Watch book.

road.hint: A message carried the whole way is worth more than the man who carried it.

options.label: Ask how the siege stands
options.outcome: "Badly, last we heard, and the last we heard was a long time ago." She looks at the stair. "If you've seen a courier, or a scroll case with our seal, it's worth more to us than to you."

options.label: Leave food for the post
options.outcome: The soldiers share it out to the crumb, by rank and then by hunger. The sergeant gives you a proper salute. Nobody has given you one in a while.
options.chronicle: Left food at a Watch post that has been waiting weeks for orders. The sergeant saluted me. It was a good salute.

road.hint: Soldiers waiting for orders eat like anyone else.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Courier'll come," says one of the soldiers. Nobody answers him.
options.chronicle: Walked past a Watch post that is still waiting for its courier. I had his case in my pack.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Courier'll come," says one of the soldiers. Nobody answers him.
options.chronicle: Walked past a Watch post that is still waiting for its courier.

name: The Brass Warden
text: An enormous construct of tarnished brass blocks the corridor, its chest glowing with banked furnace light. Etched on its torso: NONE SHALL PASS WITHOUT PROVING WORTH. A slot in its palm holds a counting board. "CHALLENGER," it says, in a voice like a bell in a cellar. "THE EXCHANGE REQUIRES PROOF OF ARITHMETIC. STAKE A QUARTER OF YOUR PURSE. LOSE, AND IT IS FORFEIT TO THE GUILD. WIN, AND THE GUILD IS GENEROUS." The Guild has not existed for four hundred years.

options.label: Answer the Warden's sums, staking a quarter of your purse

pass.outcome: The furnace in its chest flares white. "WORTH PROVEN. THE GUILD IS GENEROUS." A drawer slides out of its belly with a cog in it, warm and heavy and perfectly cut. Then, quietly, almost in a different voice: "IS THE GUILD STILL THERE?"
pass.chronicle: Out-counted the Brass Warden. It paid me in a cog, then asked whether its guild still existed. I said I did not know. I did know.

fail.outcome: It counts your coins into its chest without comment, one by one, and steps aside anyway. "THE GUILD THANKS YOU FOR YOUR CUSTOM."
fail.chronicle: Lost a quarter of my purse to a brass guard counting for a guild that died four hundred years ago. It thanked me for my custom.

road.hint: A guard that counts never forgets the sum.

options.label: Tell it the Guild is gone
options.outcome: It is still for a long time. "THEN WHO DO I GUARD FOR?" it asks. You have no answer. It steps aside. The furnace in its chest is a little dimmer as you pass.
options.chronicle: Told the Brass Warden its guild died four hundred years ago. It asked who it guards for now. I did not have an answer. It let me pass.

road.hint: Some guards are kinder left unknowing.

name: Brothers of the Deep Watch
text: Three brothers in mail under their habits keep a chapel at the head of a black stair, spears leaning by the door. Over the altar is an empty niche the size of a hand. The eldest looks at your neck before he looks at your face. "Brother Cormac?" he asks. Then he sees the answer. "Did Saint Columba come down?" The reliquary is warm against your chest.

options.label: Lay the reliquary in the niche
options.outcome: The brothers kneel. The niche takes the reliquary as if it had been cut for it, which it was. "Iona to here," the eldest says. "Two brothers, and then one stranger." He blesses you slowly and thoroughly, like a man paying a debt in full.
options.chronicle: Laid Saint Columba's relic in the chapel it was meant for. I carried it all the way down. Letting it go was harder than I expected.

road.hint: A thing carried to the end weighs nothing once it is set down.

options.label: "I lost him on the way."
options.outcome: The eldest closes his eyes. "Then he is somewhere on the stair," he says, "and the stair is ours to search." He gives you no blessing and no reproach, and goes back to his watch.
options.chronicle: Reached the chapel of the Deep Watch without Saint Columba. I had lost him on the way down. The brothers did not reproach me. The niche is still empty.

road.hint: A thing carried for others is still owed when it is lost.

options.label: Keep the reliquary
options.outcome: The brothers say nothing. The eldest looks at the empty niche, then at you, and turns his face to the wall to pray. The reliquary stays warm. It does not feel like the same warmth.
options.chronicle: Reached the chapel with Saint Columba on me and kept him there. The brothers did not argue. That was worse.

road.hint: A promise broken at the very door is the most expensive kind.

options.label: Ask for a blessing and say nothing
options.outcome: He gives it, and asks nothing. If there is a saint in your keeping, he is too polite to mention it.
options.chronicle: Asked the brothers of the Deep Watch for a blessing and did not mention what I was carrying. They were too polite to.

road.hint: A blessing asked for under false pretences still has to be lived up to.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The brothers watch you to the stair. The eldest is still looking at the empty niche.

text_variants.text: Three brothers in mail under their habits keep a chapel at the head of a black stair, spears leaning by the door. Over the altar is an empty niche the size of a hand. The eldest looks at your empty hands before he looks at your face. "Brother Cormac?" he asks. Then he sees the answer. "Did Saint Columba come down?" You have nothing to lay in it.

Three brothers in mail under their habits keep a chapel at the head of a black stair, spears leaning by the door. Over the altar is an empty niche the size of a hand. The eldest looks at your pack before he looks at your face. "Brother Cormac?" he asks. Then he sees the answer. "Did Saint Columba come down?" The reliquary is warm through your pack.

name: Last Bearer
text: A monk sits against a long oak box, his feet bound in rags. "Seven of us carried him out of Lindisfarne when the longships came," he says. "Seven years on the road. I am the one left, and I cannot manage the stairs." He takes a small red book from his habit. "This lay in the coffin with him. There is a chapel below where the brothers wait. The saint can rest here. The book should not."

options.label: Take the book and give your word

oath.what: Lay Saint Cuthbert's Gospel on the reading desk of the chapel below.

options.outcome: He puts it in your hands as if it weighed more than the coffin. "It is John's Gospel. Small enough for a pocket. People will offer you money for it on the way down. They always do." He closes his eyes, relieved of the last thing he was carrying.

thread.hint: A reading desk below is still empty.

options.chronicle: A monk of Lindisfarne trusted me with Saint Cuthbert's Gospel. I gave my word to carry it down.

road.hint: A book small enough for a pocket can still be too heavy to sell.

options.label: Share a meal with him, but refuse the errand
options.outcome: He blesses the food and then you, in that order. "No shame in knowing your load," he says. "Somebody will come." He does not sound sure.
options.chronicle: Shared a meal with the last of Saint Cuthbert's bearers, and would not carry his book. He said there was no shame in it.

options.label: Wish him well and go on
options.outcome: He nods and tucks the book back inside his habit, next to his heart, where it has been for seven years.

name: "Legitimate" Merchant
text: A goblin in an oversized merchant's coat has set up a stall using two skeletons as display racks. His wares are labeled in large, confident handwriting: "DEFINITELY NOT CURSED RING," "POTION (PROBABLY GOOD)," and "HAT (BELONGED TO SOMEONE ELSE, NOW YOURS)." "Welcome to Grix's Emporium of Totally Fine Items!" he announces. "Everything one hundred percent legal!"

options.label: Buy the "Definitely Not Cursed" item
options.outcome: Grix takes your gold with suspicious speed. The item turns out to be... fine, actually. Genuinely fine. You inspect it carefully for curses and find none. Grix watches your confusion with poorly concealed amusement. "Is being honest about dishonesty," he says philosophically, "still dishonest?"
options.chronicle: Bought a ring labelled DEFINITELY NOT CURSED. I am choosing to trust the label.

road.hint: A label that protests too much is a label.

options.label: Buy the Probably Good Potion
options.outcome: "Excellent choice," Grix says. "I tasted it myself. Three times. The last two times were to check." The potion sloshes with something enthusiastic. You pocket it, fairly confident that "probably good" is better odds than most things in this dungeon.

options.label: "I don't trust you."
options.outcome: Grix puts a hand to his chest, wounded. "Nobody trusts Grix," he says sadly. "And yet Grix is here. Every day. With his mostly fine items. For the ungrateful." He resumes polishing a skull with his sleeve as you leave.

name: Grieving Giant
text: The corridor widens dramatically to accommodate a giant sitting with its knees pulled to its chest, weeping into its enormous hands. The tears pool on the floor and small fish swim in them, fish that should not exist here, glowing faintly. "She said she'd come back," the giant says, without looking up. "That was before the dungeon was built."

options.label: Sit with it in silence (spend SP)
options.outcome: You sit on the floor beside it, in the shallow water of its grief, and say nothing. It cries for a while longer, then grows quiet. "You're still here," it says, surprised. "Most things run." It looks at you with enormous, wet eyes and breathes out something that feels like peace, and some of that peace settles into you like a cool wind.
options.chronicle: Sat with a weeping giant in a pool of his own tears. There were fish in it. I did not ask.

road.hint: Some grief makes a lake, and things live in it.

options.label: Give it something from your pack (food)
options.outcome: You offer the food upward like a small, absurd gift. The giant stares at it, then at you, then cups it in one hand and eats it with enormous, careful delicacy. "Thank you," it says. "She would have done that." It tucks one of the glowing fish into your pocket, gently. The fish dissolves into protective light.

options.label: Carefully wade past
options.outcome: You pick your way through the shallow tears, the small glowing fish parting around your boots. The giant doesn't notice, or doesn't mind. You carry the image of it for the rest of the level, all that grief, in the dark, with no one left to witness it.

name: Echo Child
text: A small figure stands at the end of the corridor, a child, you think, until you realize it has no face, only a smooth oval that reflects your expression back at you. It raises a hand in greeting. You raise yours first, you realize. It copies everything you do, a half-second later, and it is offering you something in its palm.

options.label: Accept what it offers (pay HP)
options.outcome: You reach out. It reaches out. Your hand passes through its and comes back holding something that wasn't there before, a small accessory that hums with reflected purpose. The child steps backward and folds into the wall like a shadow at noon. Your hand aches where it passed through.

options.label: Mimic it back
options.outcome: You match its every gesture perfectly. It tilts its head, you tilt yours. It steps left, you step left. After a long moment, it seems satisfied. It presses the empty space where its face should be, and suddenly you understand: it has shown you how to be unseen. The effect lasts only so long, but it's enough.
options.chronicle: Mimicked a faceless child who mimicked me first. We parted on good terms, I think.

road.hint: Whatever copies you is learning something.

options.label: Back away slowly
options.outcome: You retreat. It retreats, mirroring you. When you turn a corner it is gone. You check over your shoulder three times more than usual for the next hour.

name: The Thinking Mushroom
text: You nearly step on it before you realize it's thinking. The mushroom, enormous, bioluminescent, pulsing gently with green light, projects words directly into your mind in a calm, measured voice. "I have been considering the nature of courage for forty-three years," it tells you. "You appear to be practicing it. I find this interesting. Shall we discuss the matter?"

pass.outcome: You sit. You argue. You defend positions you didn't know you held and abandon ones you thought were certain. The mushroom is patient, precise, and devastatingly logical. Three hours pass in what feels like thirty minutes. When you stand to leave, your mind feels permanently restructured, sharper, more precise, more dangerous to itself.
pass.chronicle: Argued about courage with a mushroom that has been thinking about it for forty-three years. It conceded one point.

road.hint: Forty-three years of thought is still open to a good argument.

options.label: Ask it about the dungeon
options.outcome: "The dungeon is a question," it says. "The answer is whoever survives it."

options.label: Nod politely and keep moving
options.outcome: "Understandable," the mushroom projects, without resentment. "Courage without reflection is still courage. I wish you well." The green glow fades behind you as you walk on, and you find yourself slightly regretting the conversation you didn't have.

name: Two Mothers
text: Two women stand in the mud of a mining camp, each with a hand on the same baby. "He's mine," says one, and cries. "He's mine," says the other, and cries louder. The camp's men stand back with their arms folded, looking at you, because you carry a weapon and they don't want this. One of the women never once looks at the baby. She looks at you.

options.label: Give him to the one who weeps loudest
options.warning: One of the women never once looks at the baby. She looks at you.
options.outcome: The loud one takes him and stops crying at once, which you notice too late. The other woman sits down in the mud and does not get up.
options.chronicle: Gave a baby to whichever mother cried loudest. She stopped crying the moment she had him. The other one sat down in the mud.

road.hint: One of them never looked at the baby.

options.label: Call for a sword and offer to divide him

pass.outcome: "Cut him in two, then. Half each." One woman says, "Fair. Divide him." The other screams, "No, give him to her, only let him live." You hand the baby to the one who screamed.
pass.chronicle: Settled whose baby it was by offering to cut him in half. The right one screamed. I did not enjoy the minute before she did.

fail.outcome: You draw the sword, and the whole camp shouts, and in the noise you can't tell which cry was which. The men take the baby away to "decide among themselves".
fail.chronicle: Tried the old trick with the sword and lost my nerve and my answer at once. The camp took the baby away to decide. They will get it wrong.

road.hint: A sword in the room changes what people say.

options.label: Leave it to the camp
options.outcome: The men argue for an hour and give him to the one with the louder friends.
options.chronicle: Left two mothers and one baby to a mining camp's justice. They gave him to the woman with the louder friends.

road.hint: A camp with no judge has a crowd instead.

name: Weeping Mason
text: A translucent figure kneels beside a crumbling wall, pressing ghostly hands against the stone as if trying to repair it. He doesn't notice you at first. "Forty years," he murmurs. "Forty years and the mortar still won't hold." He built this section of the dungeon in life and cannot leave until it's perfect.

options.label: Help him find peace (offer mana)
options.outcome: You channel a little magic into the ancient stones. They glow briefly, warm and gold. The mason stares at his repaired section with trembling hands, then slowly dissolves into the air, weeping with relief. As he goes, he wraps something protective around you, the pride of a craftsman, made into a ward.
options.chronicle: Helped a ghost mason find peace after forty years of mortar that would not hold.

road.hint: Forty years of mortar is a long apology.

options.label: Ask him about the dungeon layout
options.outcome: He looks up, startled. "You can see me?" He tells you haltingly of a hidden passage three levels down and a guardian they built the dungeon around rather than disturb. He seems lighter for having told someone.

options.label: Leave him to his grief
options.outcome: You walk past quietly. Behind you, the sound of his murmuring fades, "forty years, forty years", until the dungeon swallows it whole.

name: Relic Broker
text: A neat little man has set up a folding table of bones, each labelled in a confident hand. He looks you over once, and his eyes stop at your pack. "If you should happen to be carrying something old and small and red," he says, "the brothers below would give you a blessing for it. I will give you four hundred crowns. Blessings don't buy bread."

options.label: Sell him the red book
options.outcome: He wraps it in silk with genuine love. "A wise choice," he says. "Saints don't eat."
options.chronicle: Sold Saint Cuthbert's Gospel to a relic broker for four hundred crowns. The monk who gave it to me said people would offer. He was right.

road.hint: Every relic carried down will be priced by someone on the way.

options.label: Tell him the book is promised
options.outcome: "Everything is promised to somebody," he says pleasantly, and lets you go.
options.chronicle: Told a relic broker the red book was promised. He said everything is. Not this.

road.hint: A promise refused for a price is a promise twice made.

options.label: Buy one of his vials instead, for sixty gold

name: Oracle Bones Merchant
text: An elderly woman with ink-stained fingers sits behind a low table bearing dozens of small bones, each carved with symbols. She doesn't look up when you approach. "Shang oracle bones," she says. "The real thing, not copies. I ask a question, I heat the bone, the crack gives the answer. You want to know something? The bones charge their own price."

options.label: Ask about treasure (pay gold)
options.outcome: She heats a bone over a small flame. The crack runs diagonal-right. "Favorable," she nods. "Something of value, not far. Something useful for sustaining the journey, not a weapon or a ward." She slides a small package across the table. The bones have already provided.
options.chronicle: Asked an old woman to read a cracked bone for me. The crack ran the way she said it would.

road.hint: A bone heated true cracks true.

options.label: Ask about danger ahead (pay MP)
options.outcome: She heats a different bone, older, darker. The crack branches twice. "Two dangers. One you can see, one beneath it. Don't fight the visible one first." The smoke from the bone curls into your eyes, and for a while you see the dungeon with the particular clarity of having been warned properly.

options.label: Leave the bones unasked
options.outcome: She finally looks up as you turn to go. "The bones don't mind," she says. "They've been patient for three thousand years. A few more centuries makes no difference to them."

name: The Lost Soldier
text: A soldier in armor two centuries out of fashion stands at attention in the middle of the corridor, facing a direction that is neither toward nor away from anything. "Halt," he says, without heat. "These halls are under the protection of King Aldric the Fourth." He searches your face. "You don't know that name. How long have I been standing here?"

options.label: Tell him the truth gently
options.outcome: You tell him, as carefully as you can, that King Aldric the Fourth died two hundred years ago, that his kingdom has a different name now, that the war he was guarding against ended long before his grandchildren were born. He is quiet for a long time. "Then I have kept my post well," he finally says. He salutes you with tremendous dignity and walks away into the dark.
options.chronicle: Told a soldier two centuries out of date that the war is over. He thanked me and kept standing guard.

road.hint: A soldier who never got the order to stand down is still on duty.

options.label: Pay him the soldier's tribute (gold)
options.outcome: You press coins into his gauntleted hand, the gesture of an officer paying a soldier's due. He straightens further, somehow. "King's blessing upon you, traveler." He draws a symbol in the air, and you feel it settle around you like plate armor that weighs nothing.

options.label: Walk around him quietly
options.outcome: He doesn't stop you. He seems to have already returned to whatever internal world he occupies between visitors. You glance back from the corner. He is still there, still at attention, still facing nothing.

name: Cartographer Issek
text: A compact, intensely focused woman is pinning hand-drawn maps to the wall using a knife she does not look up from. "Don't talk to me for thirty seconds," she says. Twenty-nine seconds later, she exhales and turns. "Right. Issek. I map the deep floors. I have information. You look like you have things I could use."

options.label: Trade food for her maps
options.outcome: She takes the food without ceremony and eats it standing up, already rolling a map cylinder for you. "Floors 65 through 80, approximate. Key features marked. Monsters marked where I survived long enough to mark them." The map's knowledge settles into your spatial memory like a gift.

options.label: Buy her composite survey (250 gold)
options.outcome: "The premium edition," she says without irony, and produces a map that appears to have been annotated by six different people with six different opinions about which rooms were dangerous. The synthesis of all six floods your mind, an unusually complete picture of the depths ahead.
options.chronicle: Bought a survey of the deep floors from a cartographer who pins her maps up with a knife.

road.hint: Trust a map pinned up with a knife.

options.label: "I prefer to discover things myself."
options.outcome: She shrugs with the equanimity of someone who has heard this before. "Most of the 'discover things myself' types don't make it back to update my maps." She turns back to her wall and pulls out another pin. "Good luck, though. I mean that."

name: Ormond's Granary
text: A stone granary with a barred door, scratched deep on the inside. Nobody answers when you knock. Nobody has answered for a while. The bar inside has rotted through; the door would give to a shoulder.

text_variants.text: A stone granary with a barred door, and on the step Corporal Pell, his tabard filthy now and his sword nicked, grinning like an idiot. Behind him the door is open and a grey sergeant is counting men: eleven, and Pell. "He came back," says Sergeant Ormond, as if he still can't believe it. "Ran a few floors through the dark to tell us where the way out was."

options.label: Shake Pell's hand
options.outcome: "Trembler," Pell says, "that's what they called him, that Spartan. Right?" He's still grinning. "Not me. Not any more."
options.chronicle: Found Pell at the granary with eleven living men behind him. He went back. They are calling him something better than Trembler now.

road.hint: A man who came back is more use than a man who never ran.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Pell waves you on with his nicked sword, still grinning.

options.label: Open the door
options.outcome: It gives to your shoulder, and the rotten bar with it. Inside, a journal on a sack of grain, in a sergeant's square hand. The last line: "Day nine. No runner. I hope Pell got out." You find the pencil beside it and write under it: He did.
options.chronicle: Opened a granary that had waited nine days for a runner. The sergeant's last line hoped Pell got out. I wrote under it that he did.

road.hint: The runner you send away is the runner someone else was waiting for.

options.label: Leave it barred
options.outcome: You leave the door as it is, rotten bar and all.
options.chronicle: Did not open the granary door. Some doors answer questions I did not want to ask.

name: Star Merchant
text: A small, delicate figure sits behind a fold-out table displaying glass bottles, each one containing a swirling cluster of light, constellations, captured and miniaturized. "Genuine Ursae Majoris, never used," the figure says in a voice like wind chimes. "The Pleiades, slightly incomplete. And this one, I don't know what it is. It followed me home."

options.label: Buy the unknown constellation
options.outcome: The moment the bottle leaves the merchant's hands, it uncorks itself. Light pours out and coalesces into something solid, a wand of starlight, pulsing with a frequency that matches no known school of magic. The merchant watches it go with what might be relief.
options.chronicle: Bought a constellation in a bottle. I have not opened it. I do not know what it would do.

road.hint: A sky in a bottle is still a sky.

options.label: Just browse. Move on.
options.outcome: "No pressure," the merchant says warmly. "The stars have waited this long." One of the bottles glows a little brighter as you walk away, as if wishing you luck.

name: Charon
text: A black river runs where no river should, and a flat ferry waits at a stone step, and an old man with an oar looks you up and down. "The girl you paid for," he says. "Melitta. She asked me to carry you once, free, when you came to deep water." He spits in the river. "I don't do free. I'm doing it."

options.label: Step aboard
options.outcome: The crossing is very quiet. On the far side he pushes off without a word, and then, from the middle of the river: "She says thank you. She's fine. She's better than fine."
options.chronicle: Charon ferried me across a black river for free because a drowned girl asked him to. He says she is better than fine.

road.hint: A coin paid for a stranger's crossing can buy back your own.

options.label: Decline
options.outcome: "Suit yourself," he says. "She'll be disappointed. They hate that, the dead."

name: The Cataloguing Spirit
text: A spectral figure is affixing tiny labels to the dungeon walls, to sconces, to cracks in stone, to a confused rat that sits very still under the attention. The labels read things like: "WALL (LOAD-BEARING)", "TORCH SCONCE, EMPTY, CIRCA UNKNOWN", "RAT (ALIVE, CURRENTLY)." "Oh!" the spirit says, producing a quill. "Adventurer! Encountered! Are you available to be catalogued?"

options.label: Submit to cataloguing (costs time/SP)
options.outcome: It takes extremely detailed notes. It asks your name, origin, preferred combat stance, last meal, and what you want to be remembered for. In exchange, it presses a scroll into your hands, a copy of its own dungeon index, annotated with everything it has observed and occasionally noted as "suspicious" or "structurally concerning."
options.chronicle: Let a ghost librarian catalogue me. My label says ALIVE, FOR NOW. Fair.

road.hint: Everything is catalogued eventually.

options.label: Bribe it for information (gold)
options.outcome: It takes your gold, labels it immediately ("COIN, GOLD, PROVENANCE: ADVENTURER, WARM"), and then shares its catalogued knowledge of the surrounding floors with you, a comprehensive mental map that gives you brief but useful foresight about what lies ahead.

options.label: "I don't want to be catalogued."
options.outcome: "Noted!" it says, writing furiously. You leave. Behind you, you can hear the faint sound of labeling continuing. Somewhere on these walls there is now a small sign that reads: "ADVENTURER, UNCATALOGUED, UNCOOPERATIVE."

name: Antigone
text: A young woman is scraping dirt over a dead man with her bare hands, beside a broken gate. Her nails are torn. "My brother. Creon says the dogs can have him." She doesn't stop. "Creon's edict isn't older than the unwritten laws. Nothing he writes can make it right to leave my brother to the dogs." Down the road a captain's voice carries: "A city where every sister chooses which laws to keep is no city at all. He burned our houses. Leave him."

options.label: Help her finish the burial
options.outcome: You dig together until the body is under. She says the words. Then the captain's men are at the gate, and she does not run. "Go," she says to you. "This part's mine."
options.chronicle: Helped Antigone bury her brother against the captain's edict. Then the soldiers came and she sent me away. She did not run.

road.hint: The unwritten law has a price, and someone pays it.

options.label: Go and speak for her to Creon

pass.outcome: You meet Creon on the road and put it to him: a law against burying the dead fights a law older than his city, and a ruler who wins that fight loses something worth more. He hears you out. He goes back to the gate himself, in time, and orders the burial finished with honours, and Antigone looks at him as if he were a stranger.
pass.chronicle: Talked Captain Creon round about burying a traitor. He went back in time. In the old story he was too late. I am glad of the difference.

fail.outcome: Creon hears you out, and is unmoved, and courteous about it. "The law is the city," he says, and walks on to the gate.
fail.chronicle: Argued with Captain Creon about the law of the dead. He was courteous and unmoved, and he walked on to the gate.

road.hint: A law against the dead is a quarrel with something older than the city.

options.label: Tell Creon's men where she is
options.outcome: The soldiers thank you. They do not look at you while they do it. They find her at the grave, finished, waiting.
options.chronicle: Reported Antigone to Creon's men for burying a traitor. It was the law. They did not look at me when they paid me.

road.hint: Obeying a law and agreeing with it are different things.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you she goes on scraping at the dirt with her bare hands.

name: Lantern of Regret
text: A lantern hangs at chest height in the middle of an empty corridor, hanging from nothing.
