Inside it, instead of flame, burns a small person, human-shaped, the size of your thumb, walking in tight circles and occasionally sitting down with its head in its hands. "Are you going to free me," it asks, muffled by glass, "or just stare like the others?"

options.label: Free it (pay HP, unknown consequence)
options.outcome: You break the glass with your palm, the cut is sharp and the tiny figure pours out like warm light, expanding as it goes until it's gone, dissolved into the air of the dungeon. "Thank you," says the air, softly, from everywhere at once. Something like gratitude settles around you, and the dungeon feels, briefly, like it is rooting for you.
options.chronicle: Freed a small regret from a lantern. It thanked me and walked off into the dark looking lighter.

road.hint: A regret set free is lighter for both of you.

options.label: Ask what it regrets
options.outcome: It sits down again and thinks. "I was a wish," it finally says. "Someone made me wrong, wished for something too greedy, too large, and I came out sideways. What they wanted was love. What they got was everything except it." It pauses. "Don't wish for everything. Wish for the one thing."

options.label: Leave the lantern where it hangs
options.outcome: "Understandable," it says, without bitterness. "This is usually how it goes." It resumes its small, sad circles. The lantern grows fainter as you walk away, until you can no longer tell whether the darkness behind you is shadow or simply the absence of light.

name: Neferkaptah
text: A door of black stone that was never meant to open, and opens. Inside, the air smells of river mud and myrrh. A book lies open on a bier, and where its light falls, things name themselves: your own pack murmurs the true names of the things in it, and the bones of something you killed on the way down tell you, quite clearly, what they were. Two ghosts sit at a senet board beside it: a prince in a gold collar, and a woman whose hair is still wet. A small wet footprint leads from the bier to the wall and stops. "You've come for the Book of Thoth," says the prince, and sets out the pieces. "Setne came for it too, and he was a prince." The woman does not look at the board. She looks at you.

options.label: Listen to Ahwere
options.outcome: "I am Ahwere. That is Merib's footprint; he was six." She says it quietly, the way you say a thing you have said to yourself every night for three thousand years. "My husband read one page on the boat, and he understood the birds and the fishes, and he laughed. Then Merib leaned out to see the fishes he understood, and the river took him. I went in after my son. I did not come up." She looks at the book. "Neferkaptah tied it to his chest and walked in after us. He had it. He had it all the way to the bottom." She turns back to you. "It is a true book. Every word in it is true. It costs everyone you love. Please don't take it."
options.chronicle: A drowned woman named Ahwere told me what the Book of Thoth cost her. Her son was six. There is still one small wet footprint by the wall.

road.hint: A true book can still cost more than it is worth.

options.label: Play Neferkaptah at senet for the book, staking yourself

per_miss.text: Your feet go into the stone as if it were mud. It is cold, and it is the Nile.
You are in to the waist. Your legs are a long way away, in very cold water.
The stone closes round your throat. Ahwere is the one who pulls you out.

pass.outcome: The last piece lands and Neferkaptah stares at the board as if it had cheated him. "So." He lifts the book off the bier and holds it out, and does not let go when you take it. "Then swear it, as Setne swore to me once. Read it, and bring it back. The gods will not leave you alone with it for long." Ahwere has turned her face to the wall, toward the footprint.

oath.what: Read the Book of Thoth once, then lay it on an altar so it can go home.

thread.hint: Somewhere above, a drowned woman is counting floors.

pass.chronicle: Beat a dead prince at senet for the Book of Thoth. He made me swear to bring it back once I had read it. His wife would not look at me.

fail.outcome: Neferkaptah sweeps the pieces into his hand. "Not you, then." You are waist-deep in the floor, and it lets you go only slowly, like a river letting go of a boot. The book stays on its bier.
fail.chronicle: Lost at senet to a dead prince with the Book of Thoth as the stake. The floor kept me to the waist for a while. The book stayed where it was.

road.hint: In a dead man's game the stake is always more than you put down.

0.outcome: The stone closes over your mouth. Then a wet hand takes yours and pulls, and you come up gasping on the floor above, a long way from the tomb. You will not find that black door again.
0.chronicle: Lost every round of senet for the Book of Thoth and went into the floor up to my mouth. Ahwere pulled me out. I woke a floor higher.

thread.closed_line: I never saw the tomb of Neferkaptah again. I think Ahwere made sure of it.

options.label: Leave the book, because she asked
options.outcome: You put your hands behind your back. Neferkaptah laughs, unbelieving, and then stops laughing. Ahwere gets up from the board for the first time in three thousand years and crosses to you, and puts her wet hand flat on your chest, over your heart, the way you would to feel whether someone was still alive. "Thank you," she says. "No one has ever left it." When you look back from the door, she is sitting by the small footprint on the wall, and for once she is not looking at the book.

person_status.last_line: No one has ever left it.

options.chronicle: Walked away from the Book of Thoth because a drowned mother asked me to. It is the best thing I have ever not owned.

road.hint: The greatest book in the world was guarded by a mother, and that was the true lock.

options.label: Leave the tomb
options.outcome: "Setne left too, the first time," says Neferkaptah, setting the pieces out again. Ahwere says nothing. The door closes behind you, and is a wall.
options.chronicle: Found the tomb of a prince who drowned for a book, and left. I did not decide anything. I just left.

road.hint: Leaving without choosing is still a kind of choosing.

name: Snerk Ledgerscale
text: A kobold in tiny spectacles sits at a desk made from a dragon's toenail, scratching in two ledgers at once. Beyond the arch something enormous breathes in its sleep, and gold shifts. "Snerk Ledgerscale, accountant to the Great Glaurveth. Shh." He taps the first ledger. "Her hoard." He taps the smaller one. "The villages she took it from. A coin at a time, back where it came from. Help me carry?" The second ledger has a third column, labelled, in tiny letters, ME.

options.label: Pick up a sack and help him carry
options.warning: The second ledger has a third column, labelled, in tiny letters, ME.
options.outcome: Halfway to the arch the dragon's tail twitches and lays you flat. When you get up, Snerk has gone out the other way with the sack marked ME, and you are holding the one marked VILLAGES, and an enormous eye is opening. You drop it and run.
options.chronicle: Helped a kobold carry gold out of a dragon's hoard without reading his books. He left me holding the sack. The dragon opened one eye.

road.hint: Always read the columns before you carry the sacks.

pass.outcome: Two columns add up and the third doesn't. A third of every coin "returned" has gone into ME. You point at it. Snerk goes a deeper shade of green. "Handling fees," he says. You stare at him. He crosses the column out, coin by coin, and the villages get all of it.
pass.chronicle: Audited a dragon's accountant. He was robbing the dragon for the villages, and robbing the villages for himself. Now he is only doing the first one.

fail.outcome: The columns swim. "All in order," says Snerk, closing the books a little fast. You help him carry. Halfway to the arch the dragon's tail twitches and lays you flat. When you get up, Snerk has gone out the other way with the sack marked ME, and you are holding the one marked VILLAGES, and an enormous eye is opening. You drop it and run.
fail.chronicle: Tried to audit a kobold's books and could not find the trick. Found the dragon's tail instead.

road.hint: An honest cause can still hide a dishonest column.

options.label: Take a cut to keep quiet
options.outcome: Snerk opens a fourth column, labelled YOU. "Pleasure doing business."
options.chronicle: Took a cut from a kobold who was skimming a dragon who had robbed some villages. There is a column in his book with my name on it.

road.hint: There is always room for one more column.

options.label: Leave him to his sums
options.outcome: "Shh," he says, without looking up.

name: The Merry Wanderer
text: A man in grape-leaf garlands sits on a barrel of something that definitely wasn't here before, laughing at nothing, his eyes bright as wine held up to sunlight. The dungeon around him seems fractionally more joyful, even the torches burn warmer. "Excellent timing!" he announces. "I've been waiting for someone cheerless enough to need cheering. Sit down. Drink. It's fine. It's all fine, actually."

options.label: Share food and drink with him
options.outcome: The drink tastes like three different seasons happening at once. He watches you drink it with a smile of enormous satisfaction. "There. You see? The dungeon is still terrible but you are now full of warmth. These are not unrelated facts." Your body begins knitting itself together with strange, vinous enthusiasm.
options.chronicle: Drank with a laughing stranger in a garland of grape leaves. The torches burned warmer. I think I know who he was.

road.hint: A stranger whose barrel was not there before is no stranger.

options.label: Accept his toast (free, but risky)
options.outcome: He raises his cup to you and simply says "To surviving," with complete sincerity. You don't drink anything but somehow you feel better anyway. He seems unsurprised. "Some blessings," he says, "don't need your cooperation."

options.label: "I don't drink with strangers."
options.outcome: He sighs the sigh of someone who has been hearing this since the world was young. "Every stranger," he says, "was a friend you hadn't met yet. And every friend was once a stranger you decided to trust anyway. But." He waves graciously. "Go. Be careful. Drink water at minimum."

name: Stone Singer
text: You hear the music before you see her, a deep resonant hum that makes the walls vibrate sympathetically. A woman with stone-grey skin and eyes like polished obsidian sits in a carved niche, singing to the dungeon itself. The stones seem to lean in to listen. She pauses when she sees you. "A living one. It's been so long. Do you want to hear a song?"

options.label: Ask for a song of strength
options.outcome: She sings in a frequency you feel in your bones rather than hear with your ears. The sound knits something inside you, not wounds exactly, but weariness, old damage, the slow erosion of the dungeon's weight. You walk away standing slightly straighter, your body quietly repairing itself.

options.label: Listen for free
options.outcome: She sings anyway, a slow, ancient melody about a mountain that watched a city rise and fall. When she finishes, the silence feels full rather than empty. You realize you're no longer tired. The song did something for you that sleep hadn't managed.
options.chronicle: Listened to a woman sing to the dungeon. The stones leaned in. So did I.

road.hint: Even stone listens to a good song.

options.label: Keep moving
options.outcome: She doesn't call after you. But her song follows you down three corridors, fading so slowly you aren't sure when it stops.

name: Dream Weaver
text: The figure ahead of you is weaving something from threads of silver light that seem to come from nowhere. "Dreams," she explains before you ask. "They float down here when people sleep above. I collect them, make things. Would you like to trade one of yours? You won't miss it. Probably."

options.label: Trade a dream (pay MP)
options.outcome: She reaches into your mind with two fingers, the sensation is cold and not unpleasant, and extracts something shimmering. She holds it up to her eyes. "Oh, this is a good one. You dreamed of flying." She adds it to her loom and hands you a scroll woven from finished dream-thread. You don't feel the loss, but you notice later that you can't quite remember what flight felt like.
options.chronicle: Traded a dream to a woman who weaves them. I do not remember which one. That is probably the point.

road.hint: A dream given away leaves a gap shaped like it.

options.label: Commission a dream of strength (pay gold)
options.outcome: She weaves quickly, her fingers blurring, and presses the finished piece against your forehead. You experience three seconds of a dream: you are whole, healed, standing in sunlight. When you open your eyes, some of that wholeness has stayed behind in your body. She smiles. "I do good work."

options.label: Keep your dreams to yourself
options.outcome: "Wise," she says, without irony. "Dreams are worth more than most people realize. Hold onto yours." She turns back to her loom, and the threads of light continue their slow, luminous dance.

name: Brother Sacristan
text: A side chapel, swept clean, with a lamp burning and an empty reading desk. A monk gets up from his knees so fast he knocks over the stool. "Is he coming? Is the saint coming down?" He sees your face and steadies himself. "No. Of course. The stairs. Did the bearers send anything at all?"

options.label: Lay the red book on the reading desk
options.outcome: He does not touch it at first. Then he opens it to the first line, In the beginning was the Word, and the lamp burns steadier. "You were offered money for this," he says. It is not a question.
options.chronicle: Laid Saint Cuthbert's Gospel on the desk it was meant for. The monk knew I had been offered money for it. He did not ask how much.

road.hint: A book carried to its desk is read for a thousand years.

options.label: Read the first lines aloud with him

pass.outcome: You read it together, his Latin and your stumbling, and somewhere in the third line you stop stumbling.
pass.chronicle: Read the first lines of Cuthbert's Gospel aloud with Brother Sacristan. By the third line I had stopped tripping over it.

fail.outcome: You lose your place. He finds it for you, and keeps reading.

options.label: Tell him a bearer still lives, on the floors above
options.outcome: He is out of the door before you finish, with the lamp in one hand and a blanket in the other. The chapel is dark without him, and the desk is still empty.
options.chronicle: Told Brother Sacristan the last bearer was still alive above. He ran. I still have the book.

options.label: Ask for a blessing and say nothing about any book
options.outcome: He gives it gladly and asks nothing. If there is a small red book in your pack, it grows no lighter.

name: The Pardoner
text: A man with long yellow hair and a voice like a goat sits on a pack of relics outside a pilgrims' camp: a glass of pig's bones, a pillowcase he swears is Our Lady's veil, a sheaf of pardons sealed hot from Rome. He winks at you. "My text is always the same, friend. The love of money is the root of all evil. Never fails." He nods at the pilgrims. "Tell them you saw a miracle by my bones, and I'll split the take with you."

options.label: Tell the pilgrims you saw a miracle
options.outcome: The pilgrims empty their purses into his cap, weeping with joy. He splits it with you very fairly, which is the only honest thing he does all day.
options.chronicle: Swore to a camp of pilgrims that a pig's bones worked a miracle. The Pardoner split the take fairly. He preached against greed while he did it.

road.hint: Every fraud needs a witness, and the witness is paid in the same coin.

options.label: Refuse him
options.outcome: "Pity," he says. "You have an honest face. It would have been worth a fortune." He goes to preach anyway, and does fairly well without you.
options.chronicle: Refused to lend my face to a pardoner. He said it would have been worth a fortune. He did fairly well without it.

road.hint: An honest face is worth a fortune to exactly the wrong people.

options.label: Show the pilgrims his pardons are forged

pass.outcome: Every pardon is "given at Rome" and dated in the reign of a Pope who had been dead for a hundred years when the seal was cut. You read out the date and the name, and the Pope's dates, and an old pilgrim who once walked to Rome starts to laugh, and then they all do. The Pardoner packs his pig's bones with great dignity and leaves.
pass.chronicle: Showed a camp of pilgrims that their pardons were dated in the reign of a dead Pope. They laughed the Pardoner out. His minders hit me first.

fail.outcome: You get the Pope wrong, and he corrects you, beautifully, in front of everyone. The pilgrims buy twice as much.
fail.chronicle: Tried to catch a pardoner out on the date of his pardons and got the Pope wrong myself. His minders hit me, and the pilgrims bought double.

road.hint: A pardon dated in a dead man's reign is pardoning nobody.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you the Pardoner starts his sermon. The love of money is the root of all evil. It never fails.

name: Weeping Mother
text: She appears slowly, the outline first, then the tears that fall like silver and vanish before they reach the stone. A glowing locket circles her like a small moon. "My boy, Pip. He was nine. He went in after the dog, and the dog came back without him." Her voice breaks. "Will you pray with me? Not for him. For me. I'm so tired. I just want to stop looking."

options.label: Kneel and pray with her until she can rest
options.outcome: The prayer goes on and on. Her tiredness presses down on you like a stone, twelve years of walking. When you finish, her tears have slowed. "I can feel it," she breathes. "Peace. After so long." She goes into warm light, smiling, and the locket goes with her.
options.chronicle: Prayed with a ghost named Maud until she could rest. Her boy went in after a dog twelve years ago. The dog came back. She has stopped looking now.

road.hint: Some searches end not in finding, but in being allowed to stop.

options.label: Tell her that her love has outlasted death
options.outcome: She flickers. "Thank you for seeing me. Most walk right through." She keeps searching. She will always keep searching.

name: Andvari
text: A pool under a waterfall, and in it a great pike that watches you with an old man's eyes. On the rock beside the pool lies a net of grey silk, the kind Ran uses to drown sailors. Someone has carved a sign on the rock in neat runes: ANDVARI'S POOL. THE GOLD IS UNDER HIM. THE NET IS HOW. The pike does not swim away. It looks very tired of this.

options.label: Net him and take all his gold, ring and all
options.outcome: He comes up as a dwarf, dripping and furious, and gives you everything, as he once gave Loki everything. Then, very quietly: "The ring will be the death of whoever holds it. It has never failed yet."
options.chronicle: Netted a dwarf in a pool and took his gold and his little ring. He told me it would be the death of whoever held it. It is a very good ring.

road.hint: A curse that killed a dragon is not afraid of you.

options.label: Take the net and leave him be
options.outcome: You roll up the grey silk. It is lighter than it looks and colder than water. The pike watches it go into your pack and sinks a little lower, the way a man sits down when he knows the next visitor will come with it.
options.chronicle: Took Ran's net off the rock by Andvari's pool and left the dwarf alone. Nobody can net him with it now, except whoever I give it to.

road.hint: A net taken from the rock is still a net.

options.label: Throw the net into the waterfall, so nobody can use it again
options.outcome: The grey silk goes down the falls and is gone. The pike comes up as a dwarf, slowly, and sits on the rock and looks at you for a long time. "Loki didn't do that," he says. Then he tells you something about Fafnir: that a dragon's armour is all on top, and that he crawls to the water every evening along the same groove in the rock.
options.chronicle: Threw Ran's net into the waterfall so nobody could rob Andvari again. He came up as a dwarf and told me where Fafnir is soft.

road.hint: The net is how. Without the net, there is no how.

outcome_variants.outcome: The grey silk goes down the falls and is gone. The pike comes up as a dwarf, slowly, and sits on the rock and looks at you for a long time. "Loki didn't do that," he says. Then he sniffs, and smells the dragon on you. "And Fafnir's dead, isn't he? Then there's nobody left on my gold but me." He laughs, a little, for the first time in a long time.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Threw Ran's net into the waterfall so nobody could rob Andvari again. He came up as a dwarf, smelled Fafnir's blood on me, and laughed.

name: Swift Stranger

tells: two small pinions tucked in the band
a staff with two snakes carved round it

text: A young man leans against the wall with his arms crossed, grinning like he knows a joke that hasn't been told yet. His traveller's hat has two small pinions tucked in the band. He carries a staff with two snakes carved round it, and one of them blinks. A tortoise shell with strings hangs on his back. "I left something for you at a crossroads," he says. "Probably. Or I will have. Want to make a trade?"

text_variants.text: A young man leans against the wall with his arms crossed, grinning like he knows a joke that hasn't been told yet. His traveller's hat has two small pinions tucked in the band. He carries a staff with two snakes carved round it, and one of them blinks. A tortoise shell with strings hangs on his back. "I left something for you at a crossroads," he says. "Probably. Or I will have. Want to make a trade?" 'We've met. You watched my father's pitcher. He's still talking about it.'

options.label: Trade food for his gift
options.outcome: He sniffs it approvingly and flicks a feather from his hat at your boots. It dissolves into the leather. Each step lands further than it should.
options.chronicle: Traded my lunch to a grinning stranger for a feather that went into my boots. I have been walking too fast ever since.

options.label: Ask whether Apollo ever got his cattle back

pass.outcome: He laughs so hard he has to hold the wall. "I was one day old. I walked them backwards so the tracks pointed the wrong way, then made the lyre to pay him off." He taps the tortoise shell. "Clever mortal."

delayed.text: Where two corridors cross, a wand lies on the flagstones, tied with a ribbon in the shape of a winged sandal.

pass.chronicle: Asked a grinning stranger about some stolen cattle. He laughed so hard he had to hold the wall. Then he left me a present at a crossroads.

fail.outcome: "Cattle?" He looks innocent, which on him is a warning. When he's gone, you count your purse twice. It is all there, which is somehow worse.

road.hint: A thief who invented music will always tell you how he did it.

options.label: "You're a long way from Olympus, Messenger."
options.outcome: He tips the hat to you with real respect. "Most of them only look at the sandals." He is gone before the hat comes back down.
options.chronicle: Called a grinning stranger by his proper title. He tipped his hat and vanished before it came back down.

options.label: Decline the trade
options.outcome: "Fair enough. You're the careful type. I respect that. Mostly." He saunters off whistling something that sounds like it has not been written yet.

name: Azarias
text: A young man with a travelling staff and a dog at his heels falls into step beside you as if you had arranged it. "Azarias, son of the great Ananias, one of your own kin." The dog wags at you as if you were an old friend. He has a fish wrapped in leaves under his arm and talks about it a great deal. He breaks a loaf of his own and offers you half. He holds his half while he talks, and later it is gone, though you never see him eat.

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the second stair he stops. 'This is as far as I was sent.' He gives you a pouch with the fish's gall in it, wrapped in a leaf. 'For eyes that have stopped seeing. You'll know.'
on_arrive.chronicle: Walked two floors with a young man called Azarias and his dog. He never stepped on a trap and never ate a thing. He left me a fish's gall for someone's eyes.

on_fail.outcome: Azarias is simply not there any more, and nor is the dog.
on_fail.chronicle: Lost track of Azarias and his dog on the stairs. I do not think he was lost. I think I was.

options.label: Walk with him a while
options.outcome: "Good," he says. "It's better with company. The dog agrees."

road.hint: A guide who never eats is not travelling on bread.

options.label: Ask him what the fish is for

pass.outcome: "The heart and liver, burned, drive off a demon. The gall heals eyes." He looks at you sidelong. "You know the story."
pass.chronicle: A travelling man with a dog told me what a fish's gall is good for. He seemed pleased I knew the story already.

fail.outcome: "Supper," he says, and the dog sneezes.

road.hint: Some fish are carried for reasons other than supper.

options.label: "You haven't eaten all day, Azarias."
options.outcome: He laughs, and for a moment there is more light in the corridor than there are torches. "I am Raphael, one of the seven who stand before the Lord. All this way you only thought you saw me eat." He blesses you with two fingers, the way a priest does, and the dog wags.
options.chronicle: Told my travelling companion he had not eaten all day. He laughed and said his name was Raphael. The dog was not surprised.

options.label: "I travel alone."
options.outcome: "Then go with God," he says, "and mind the third step." There is a trap on the third step.

name: The Mast
text: A ship has run its bow onto the shingle at your feet, black water all round its stern, and a man is lashed to its mast hand and foot. You could climb aboard. Somewhere across the lake voices are singing, and it is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard. His crew sit at the oars with wax in their ears. The man strains at the ropes, weeping. "Cut me loose. I'm the captain. I order it. I'll die if I don't hear the end." Scratched into the mast in his own hand: WHATEVER I SAY, DON'T.

pass.outcome: The ropes part and he lunges for the water, and you get an arm round him and hold on, and say his own words back to him: whatever I say, don't. Which captain gives the orders, the one who wrote that, or the one shouting now? He stops straining. He stays on the deck, shaking, until the song ends.
pass.chronicle: Cut a captain free from his mast and then held him to his own written orders. He stayed. I am not sure I would have.

fail.outcome: He goes over the side before you can say anything at all. The song stops a moment later, as if satisfied.
fail.chronicle: Cut a captain loose from his mast because he begged. He went into the water. The singing stopped, satisfied.

road.hint: When a man's two selves disagree, ask which one wrote the orders.

options.label: Keep him bound
options.outcome: He curses you, and then begs, and then curses you again, until the song stops. Then he goes limp in the ropes. "Thank you," he says. "That was the worst hour of my life, and I would not give it back."
options.chronicle: Kept a captain tied to his mast while the Sirens sang. Afterwards he said it was the worst hour of his life and he would not give it back.

road.hint: Sometimes the kindest thing is to obey the man he was an hour ago.

options.label: Listen to the end of the song yourself
options.outcome: It promises you everything, every answer, everything that has ever happened. You come to waist-deep in black water with the captain screaming your name from the mast. You remember almost none of it. Almost.
options.chronicle: Listened to the Sirens to the end. Came to in the lake up to my waist. I remember one line of it. I am not writing it down.

road.hint: A song that promises every answer charges for the hearing.

options.label: Stop your ears and walk on
options.outcome: You walk on with your fingers in your ears. The song follows you a long way, and then it doesn't.

name: Neferkaptah
text: The torches on this floor burn blue. Water is coming up through the cracks in the floor, and it smells of river mud and myrrh. Neferkaptah walks out of the wall in his gold collar, and behind him come the tomb's dead, wrapped and silent, more than you want to count. "You swore," he says. "You read it. I can smell it on you." Behind them all, a long way back, a woman with wet hair is standing very still, and does not come closer.

text_variants.text: The torches on this floor burn blue. Water is coming up through the cracks in the floor, and it smells of river mud and myrrh. Neferkaptah walks out of the wall in his gold collar, and behind him come the tomb's dead, wrapped and silent, more than you want to count. "You swore," he says. "You never even opened it. You carried my book all this way and never once looked inside." For a moment he sounds more hurt than angry. Behind them all, a long way back, a woman with wet hair is standing very still, and does not come closer.

options.label: Give the book back
options.outcome: He takes it and holds it against his chest, where the linen band was. The dead go back into the walls one by one. Ahwere is the last to go. She does not say anything. She does not need to.
options.chronicle: The dead came for the Book of Thoth because I was late returning it. I gave it back. Ahwere watched. I would rather she had shouted.

road.hint: A loan returned late is still returned, but the lender remembers.

options.label: "I don't have it any more."
options.outcome: "Then you will bring me to where it is," he says, "or you will come with me to where I am." The water rises over your boots.
options.chronicle: Told a drowned prince I no longer had his book. He did not care where it was, only that I had sworn. His dead came up out of the floor.

road.hint: A promise to the dead is owed by the promiser, not by the pocket.

options.label: Refuse. The book is yours now
options.outcome: "Then you'll keep it the way I kept it," he says, and the water rises over your boots.
options.chronicle: Refused to give the Book of Thoth back to the prince I swore to. His dead came up out of the floor. I kept the book. The water is still in my boots.

road.hint: A promise to the dead is collected by the dead.

name: Socrates
text: A cell with the door open and a jailer asleep, and inside a snub-nosed old man in a worn cloak, cheerfully barefoot. A cup sits on the sill, waiting for the watch to change. A worried friend wrings his hands. "Crito has a boat waiting," Socrates says. "He thinks I should run. I think I shouldn't. Show me I'm wrong and I'll go." He pats the bench. "But you'll have to show me. I'm very annoying about that."

options.label: Argue with him, staking your strength

pass.outcome: You argue until the torches burn low, and twice he has to stop and think, and once he laughs out loud and says, "Oh, that's good." When the watch changes he still drinks the cup. "You nearly had me," he says. "Nearly is the most anyone has ever got. Thank you for the best argument I've had in a month."
pass.chronicle: Argued with Socrates for hours about whether he should run. I nearly had him. He drank the cup anyway and said it was his best argument in a month.

fail.outcome: He takes your argument apart so gently you hardly notice until you have nothing left to stand on. "Don't be sad," he says. "That's the useful part." You are wrung out.
fail.chronicle: Argued with Socrates and lost every point, very politely. I have never been so tired or learned so much.

road.hint: An argument lost to the right person leaves you richer.

options.label: Carry him out by force
options.outcome: He doesn't fight. He just keeps talking, all the way to Crito's boat on the black water, about whether a man carried away against his will has escaped at all. Crito weeps with relief. You watch the boat pull away. Socrates looks back at his cell until the dark takes it.
options.chronicle: Carried Socrates out of his cell to Crito's boat. He talked the whole way about whether it counted. He looked back at his cell until the dark took it.

road.hint: You can carry a man out of a cell and not out of his reasons.

options.label: Stay for the last conversation
options.outcome: You stay. He talks about the soul and asks you questions you will be answering for years. When the watch changes he drinks, and walks about until his legs are heavy, and lies down. "Crito," he says at the very end, "we owe a cock to Asclepius. Don't forget."
options.chronicle: Stayed with Socrates to the end. His last words were about a debt of a chicken. He did not want it forgotten. Neither do I.

road.hint: The last thing a wise man remembers may be a small debt.

name: Thorleif Grimsson
text: A man with a harp across his knees sits against a wall that is white with frost in the shape of a hand. The frost is on him, too, from the chest down. He is perfectly calm. "Thorleif. Skald. A draugr shook my hand; I'll not see the morning." He smiles. "My brother Eyvind went over the edge of the Long Dark. There's a stone there with room on it. I made him a verse. Will you carve it for me? I'll teach it to you. It's short. He was not a patient man."

options.label: Learn the verse and swear to carve it
options.outcome: He teaches it to you three times, beating the time on the harp. Eyvind went where the dark goes down; no mead, no fire, no brother's hand. Stone, say his name to the wind that stays. "Good," he says. "Now you're a skald. A bad one. It'll do."

oath.what: Carve his verse for his brother Eyvind on the rune-stone at the Long Dark.

thread.hint: A verse in my head is waiting for a stone.

options.chronicle: Learned a dead skald's verse for his brother by heart and swore to carve it on the stone at the Long Dark. He said I was a bad skald. It will do.

road.hint: A verse carried in your head weighs nothing and is still a load.

options.label: Give him a healing potion for the cold
options.outcome: It warms his face and hands, and does nothing at all for the frost. "That's good," he says. "Now I can feel my fingers to play."

options.label: Ask him to play while there's time
options.outcome: He plays the verse for his brother, and then a long, bad, funny song about a goat, and then he stops in the middle of a line.
options.chronicle: A dying skald played me a verse for his brother and then a terrible song about a goat. He stopped in the middle of a line.

name: Pellok the Very Lost
text: A merchant in a wine merchant's apron is sitting on a crate labeled FINE VINTAGES, looking at a map upside-down with tremendous concentration. He does not hear you until you are quite close. "GAH. Oh. Sorry. Sorry. Do you, is this the 40th floor? I was told there was a marketplace on the 40th floor. I am very much getting the sense it was not on the 40th floor."

options.label: Buy a bottle from him (100 gold)
options.outcome: He is so relieved to make a sale that he nearly hugs you. The wine is, inexplicably, excellent, a deep red that tastes of a summer several decades ago and warms you to the marrow. Your wounds respond favorably to the vintage. He marks you on his route map as a 'reliable customer.'

options.label: Give him food to help him back up
options.outcome: He accepts the food with enormous gratitude. "You are a saint. A genuine saint. Here, take this, I've been using it as a paperweight. The previous owner said it was powerful. They were very confident about it." He presses a potion into your hands and begins the long walk upward, muttering.

options.label: Point him vaguely upward
options.outcome: "Up," he repeats, as though this had not occurred to him. "Yes. That, that tracks. Thank you. Tremendous. Right." He hoists his crate, takes two steps in the wrong direction, corrects himself, and begins a very long journey home.
options.chronicle: Pointed a lost wine merchant upward. He is sixty floors off. I hope he has a lot of wine.

road.hint: Some merchants are lost on purpose by their maps.

name: Alchemist Mourne
text: An alchemist has set up a field laboratory in what was once a guardroom, surrounded by equipment that should not survive this far down. Her goggles glow faintly green. "Oh, a live one. Excellent. I've been working on something that needs a test subject, and before you refuse, I'm offering fair compensation. I'm an alchemist, not a monster."

options.label: Volunteer as test subject
options.outcome: The compound tastes of copper and overripe plums. There is a moment of alarming internal heat, then it passes. "Excellent. Tissue response nominal. Better than nominal, actually." She scribbles notes while your body begins to quietly repair itself, wounds knitting at a rate you find both reassuring and slightly uncanny.
options.chronicle: Volunteered for a deep alchemist's experiment. I regenerate now, briefly. She took notes.

road.hint: A test subject is paid in results.

options.label: Buy her regeneration salve (200 gold)
options.outcome: "Tested and approved," she says, by which she means tested on herself, which you realize when she pulls up her sleeve to show old burn scars in various stages of alchemical healing. The salve is thick and smells terrible and works immediately.

options.label: "Hard pass."
options.outcome: "Noted," she says, without offense. "Healthy skepticism of unsolicited chemistry. Good instinct, actually. Come back if you change your mind, I'll be here until I run out of subjects or the dungeon runs out of patience with me." She returns to her bubbling apparatus.

name: Sir Lorvaine the Certain
text: A knight in immaculate but deeply outdated armour stands squarely in your path. "I am Sir Lorvaine the Certain, and I have a riddle. If you answer correctly, I will share with you the gifts of my failed quest. If you answer incorrectly, I will also share them. The riddle is mostly a formality at this point. I'm very lonely."

pass.outcome: You answer it. Sir Lorvaine stares at you, then sits down on the floor in his armour with a great clang. "Forty-seven years," he says. "Nobody's ever got it. I can stop composing them now." He looks lighter than he has in decades.
pass.chronicle: Answered Sir Lorvaine's riddle. Nobody had in forty-seven years. He sat down on the floor and said he could finally stop writing them.

fail.outcome: He declares you correct anyway, with enormous ceremony, and gives you the accessory.
fail.chronicle: Got Sir Lorvaine's riddle wrong. He declared me correct anyway. He is very lonely.

road.hint: Some riddles are asked only to be answered at last.

options.label: Wish him well and continue
options.outcome: "Of course," he says, very slightly too loud. You hear him composing a new riddle as you walk away.

name: The Last Champion
text: A massive warrior sits polishing armor that no longer has a purpose to be polished for. He does it anyway, with the methodical attention of someone who has run out of things to do but not out of discipline. He looks up at you and something wakes behind his eyes. "Still coming down, are they? Good. The deep floors need witnesses."

options.label: Ask him to train you for a while
options.outcome: He trains you hard and without mercy, correcting your grip and your footwork and the angle of your shoulders with the blunt precision of a man who was taught by people who learned the hard way. An hour passes like a grinding stone. When he's done, he taps your weapon. "There. It knows how to be held properly now."
options.chronicle: Trained with an old champion polishing armour for a kingdom that no longer exists. He was glad of the work.

road.hint: Discipline outlives the kingdom it served.

options.label: Share a meal with him
options.outcome: He receives the food with the dignity of a man who has forgotten what it means to receive anything. He eats slowly. "My first meal shared in..." He counts. Stops counting. "Thank you." He refills something in your pack, rations you didn't know you were missing. "You'll need it more than I do."

options.label: "What are you still guarding?"
options.outcome: He looks down at the armor in his hands. The question takes a long time to reach an answer. "The idea," he finally says, "that someone should still be here when the next one comes through. So they know the road has been walked before." He gestures you onward. "It has been walked before."

name: Squire Tobyn
text: A squire of about sixteen sits on a broken step with a wooden practice sword across his knees, watching the stair you came down. He stands up too fast when he sees you. "Is Ser Brennan behind you? He said he'd catch up. He always catches up."

options.label: Give him the sword, and Ser Brennan's message
options.outcome: He takes the sword the way Brennan held it out, hilt first, before he understands. Then he understands. "He said I was ready?" You nod. He cries the way boys do when they're trying not to, and then he stops, and buckles it on.
options.chronicle: Gave Squire Tobyn his knight's sword and told him he was not left behind. He buckled it on before he had finished crying.

road.hint: A message from the dead is the one delivery that cannot wait.

options.label: Give him Ser Brennan's message, without the sword
options.outcome: You tell him what Brennan said, and then you have to tell him the rest: the sword is gone, lost on the way down. He listens to all of it. "Ready," he says. "He said ready." He picks up the wooden sword, and holds it differently.
options.chronicle: Gave Squire Tobyn his knight's last words but not his sword. I had lost it on the way down. He took the words anyway.

road.hint: A dead man's words can be delivered even when his steel cannot.

options.label: Keep the sword. Tell him Brennan fell, nothing more
options.outcome: "Fell." He nods slowly. "Then I'll wait for his body." He is still sitting on the step when you look back.
options.chronicle: Told Brennan's squire his knight fell, and kept the sword. He is still waiting on that step. I gave my word to a dying man and broke it to a boy.

road.hint: A promise to the dead is broken in front of the living.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "He'll catch up," Tobyn says, mostly to himself.

name: The Lingering Echo
text: A figure composed entirely of slowly dispersing arcane notation flickers in the center of the corridor, the echo of a wizard who died mid-incantation. The echo loops: hand raised, mouth forming a word, then reset, raised again, the same word. It notices you and breaks the loop with visible effort. "I require... a conduit. Brief. I have knowledge yet to spend."

options.label: Let the echo channel through you
options.outcome: The sensation is like holding a lightning bolt by the wrong end. Decades of arcane study pour through your nervous system in seconds, most of it incomprehensible, but the raw magical energy saturates you. The echo completes its word at last, a single syllable of great satisfaction, and disperses. Your mana swells with the residue.
options.chronicle: Let the echo of a dead wizard finish his spell through me. It was a long word.

road.hint: A word left half spoken waits for a mouth.

options.label: Offer a scroll as a vessel instead
options.outcome: The echo examines the scroll with something like hope. It pours itself into the parchment in a cascade of luminous script. The scroll blackens and crumbles, used up, but in its place a wand assembles itself from notation and will, solid as steel, humming with the dead wizard's last intent.

options.label: Leave the echo in peace
options.outcome: You step carefully around the looping figure. Behind you, the hand raises, the mouth forms the word, and resets. Raises. Resets. Some spells take longer to finish than their casters do.

name: Rune-Stone
text: A standing stone at the edge of a great dark drop, carved with runes in a ribbon that ends in a serpent's head. Most of the ribbon is full: names, and who raised the stone for whom. The last loop is empty. Somebody has left a chisel in a crack, as if they knew someone would need it.

options.label: Carve Thorleif's verse for his brother
options.outcome: You carve it the way he said it, line by line, the serpent's head last. When you step back the stone looks finished, the way a sentence does when it has its full stop. Far below in the dark, someone laughs, the way a brother laughs.
options.chronicle: Carved Thorleif's last verse on the rune-stone for his brother, as I swore. It took an hour and all my patience. The stone looks finished now.

road.hint: A stone with an empty loop is waiting for somebody's words.

options.label: Carve your own name in the empty loop instead
options.outcome: It looks very good there. Anyone who comes this way will read it and wonder who you were. Nobody will ever read Thorleif's.
options.chronicle: Carved my own name on the rune-stone in the place I promised to a dead skald. It looks very good. I am trying not to read it.

road.hint: A stone remembers whoever cut it, and whoever was left off.

name: Lady Bertilak
text: In a warm hall cut into the rock, a lady in green sits by a fire, winding a sash of green silk round her fingers. "My lord said whatever you win in his house, you give to him before you leave. Those are the terms." She holds out the sash. "This is a girdle no blade can cut through. You go to meet the Green Knight soon. He will swing at your neck." She smiles. "My lord need never know."

options.label: Take it and keep it secret
options.outcome: She ties it round your waist herself. At the door her husband asks what you won in his house. You tell him: nothing.
options.chronicle: Took a lady's green girdle against the Green Knight's axe and did not tell her husband. The terms were plain. I wanted to live.

road.hint: A secret kept from your host goes with you to the chapel.

options.label: Take it, and give it to your host at the door, as agreed
options.outcome: Her husband turns the sash over in his hands, laughing, and does not give it back. "Honest," he says. "We'll see how honest the Knight finds your neck."
options.chronicle: Was given a girdle that would save my neck, and handed it to my host because those were his terms. He laughed. I hope the Knight is as amused.

road.hint: Keeping a bargain you could break unseen is the whole test.

options.label: Refuse it
options.outcome: She winds the sash back round her fingers. "Gawain took it," she says. "He was very nearly perfect." She seems disappointed in you, and impressed, at once.
options.chronicle: Refused a girdle that would have saved my neck from the Green Knight. The lady said Gawain took it. I am not Gawain.

road.hint: The gift that saves your life can cost you something you meant to keep.

name: Vafthrudnir
text: A hall of ice-black stone, and a giant on a high seat with a beard like frozen rope. A row of skulls on the shelf behind him, each labelled in runes. "Vafthrudnir. I know more than anyone who has ever sat on that bench." He points at it. "Sit, and we'll trade questions. Lose, and your head goes on the shelf. Win, and you'll carry home more than you came with."

pass.outcome: He sits back. He has run out of questions, and you have not. "Take your head home," he says slowly. "And some of mine."
pass.chronicle: Traded questions with Vafthrudnir for my head, and won. He gave me some of his on the way out.

fail.outcome: "Close," he says, and takes his fee. It is not your whole head. It is enough.
fail.chronicle: Lost a contest of questions to Vafthrudnir. He kept a piece of me on his shelf, labelled. I would rather not know what the label says.

road.hint: Never stake your head against someone with a shelf.

options.label: Play a short contest for coin instead
"What did Odin whisper in Baldr's ear on the pyre?"

pass.outcome: The giant's face goes grey. Nobody has ever asked him that. Nobody alive knows the answer, and he has just realised who taught you to ask. "You've been talking to a one-eyed man," he says, and gets up from his seat, and gives it to you.
pass.chronicle: Asked Vafthrudnir the one question nobody can answer. He went grey and gave me his seat. I had it from a one-eyed man at a well.

outcome_variants.outcome: The giant's face goes grey. Nobody has ever asked him that. Nobody alive knows the answer, and he has just realised where you learned to ask. "You've been drinking at Mimir's well," he says, and gets up from his seat, and gives it to you.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Asked Vafthrudnir the one question nobody can answer. He went grey and gave me his seat. I had it from the water of Mimir's well.

fail.outcome: You fumble the question you came to ask. He laughs, and lets you go anyway, and the laugh follows you out.

road.hint: Some contests are won by remembering who you met at a well.

name: Crossroads Fiddler

tells: one of his boots is the wrong shape

text: A gentleman in a black coat sits on a milestone where four corridors meet, tuning a fiddle. He smells of good cologne and, under it, of struck matches. "Tired of being asked questions? Everyone down here is quizzing you. Sign, and the answers will come to you sooner, from here to the bottom." He holds out a paper covered in very small print, and a pen. One of his boots is the wrong shape, as if there were no toes in it. "Payment later. Much later."

options.label: Sign
options.outcome: The ink is warm. He plays you a little tune to celebrate, and it is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard, and you know you will never hear the end of it. Answers start arriving in your head a moment before the questions do. It is not a comfortable feeling.
options.chronicle: Signed a gentleman's paper at a crossroads so the answers would come to me sooner. Now they come early. So, I suspect, will the bill.

road.hint: A shortcut through every test is still a test.

options.label: Read the small print before you decide

pass.outcome: It takes a while, because the print gets smaller as it goes, but there it is in the last line, in a hand like a scratch: and the signatory's name, in the book that is not kept by the Other Fellow. You look up. He is already smiling, a little ruefully. You tear the paper in half, and then in quarters. "Some other crossroads," he says, and there is a scorch mark on the milestone where he sat.
pass.chronicle: Read the small print on a crossroads gentleman's contract and found my name in the wrong book. I tore it up. He left a scorch mark.

fail.outcome: The print swims. He leans over helpfully and reads it to you, beautifully, every clause sounding perfectly reasonable. Then he holds out the pen again.

road.hint: The price of a bargain is always in the smallest letters.

options.label: Refuse without reading
options.outcome: "No." He folds the paper into his coat without argument. "There's always a next crossroads," he says, and goes back to tuning.
options.chronicle: Told a gentleman at a crossroads I would not sign his paper. I never did find out what was in it.

road.hint: A no without reading is still a no, but you never learn what you refused.

options.label: Walk past without a word
options.outcome: He plays a few bars after you. You find you are walking in time to them for a while.

name: Something in a Bottle
text: A large bottle sits in the middle of the corridor, sealed with a wax stamp bearing a warning in three dead languages. It is rattling. A voice from inside says, with considerable dignity: "I am aware of how this looks. I am also aware that you can hear me. I propose a negotiation."

options.label: Open the bottle
options.outcome: The wax seal resists until it doesn't, scoring your hands. The djinn emerges as a column of pressurized wind and hangs in the air, composing itself. "Thank you. That was embarrassing. A gift, for your trouble." It blows through you, and your body hums with speed you cannot quite contain.
options.chronicle: Opened a bottle that asked very politely to be opened. It was polite about leaving, too.

road.hint: Politeness through glass proves very little.

options.label: Negotiate through the glass (150 gold)
options.outcome: You slide coins under the bottle's lip. The djinn inside makes a sound of elaborate exasperation. "I cannot actually use gold in here. But I appreciate the gesture." It exhales a breath of pure arcane through the glass. Your mana replenishes itself through some mechanism you decline to examine.

options.label: Leave the bottle sealed
options.outcome: "Sensible," the bottle says. "Genuinely. I have been in here a very long time and my temperament is not at its best. You made the correct call." The rattling resumes as you walk away.

name: Grey-Eyed Woman

tells: eyes the grey of storm clouds
an owl that is not quite an owl
a spear propped like a broom

text: A woman stands in the corridor as if the dungeon were built around her. Her eyes are the grey of storm clouds before lightning, and an owl that is not quite an owl sits on her shoulder. A spear is propped against the wall beside her like a broom. The air smells faintly of olives. "You are further down than most," she says. "I am curious whether your mind has sharpened to match your ambition."

options.label: Ask whether Arachne's tapestry had a single flaw

pass.outcome: Her eyes go the grey of a storm about to break. "No," she says at last. "Not one. That was the problem." The owl hoots once, as if at a joke. "Most mortals ask what lies at the bottom. You asked the one question I still think about." She touches your eyelids.
pass.chronicle: Asked a grey-eyed woman whether a certain weaver's work had any flaw. She said no, and that was the problem. I see more clearly now.

fail.outcome: "A foolish question," she says, and the owl looks away from you.
fail.chronicle: Asked a grey-eyed woman about a weaver. The owl looked away. I have been looked away from by better birds.

road.hint: Ask a proud goddess about her rival, and see what her face does.

options.label: "Grey-eyed Pallas. You're a long way from Athens."
options.outcome: "And you are a long way from home." She almost smiles. "Go on. I want to see how this ends."
options.chronicle: Named the grey-eyed woman to her face. She almost smiled and said she wanted to see how my story ends. So do I.

options.label: "What lies at the bottom?"
options.outcome: She tilts her head. "A question. Good." The owl blinks slowly. "At the bottom lies the thing that asked itself what lies above. Everything looks up, child. Even the abyss has ambitions."

options.label: Bow and pass
options.outcome: She inclines her head, a gesture that carries more weight than any blessing you can name. The owl watches you out of sight.

name: The Unseen Archivist
text: Nothing is there. And yet: the sound of a quill scratching on parchment. A throat cleared politely. The faint impression of a chair being occupied. "I catalog the deeds of those who descend," says a voice at desk-height, precisely where no desk is. "I have questions, if you have answers. And I pay for my interviews."

options.label: Agree to be interviewed
options.outcome: The interview is thorough. It asks about your earliest memory, your greatest fear, your theory on what lies at the dungeon's bottom, and whether you prefer mornings. It transcribes your answers with the focused energy of someone who finds all answers equally important. When it finishes, a purse of gold appears on the floor in front of you. "Excellent data," it says warmly. "Truly."
options.chronicle: Was interviewed by an archivist I could not see. My answers are now in a book somewhere.

road.hint: Someone is always writing it down.

options.label: Ask who it archives for
options.outcome: A long pause. The quill stops. "That is the question," it says, and you hear something that might be a smile in the voice. "Isn't it. The honest answer is: I archive for myself. I have been doing this long enough that 'for whom' stopped mattering and 'that it is done' took its place." The quill resumes.

options.label: Decline the interview
options.outcome: "Noted," says the voice, and you hear your refusal being noted. "That is, itself, a data point. Walk safe." The scratching of the quill follows you down the corridor for longer than seems possible, then stops all at once.

name: The Mirror Shade
text: The figure ahead looks exactly like you, or how you looked before the descent. Cleaner. Less scarred. It smiles with your face. "You have come a long way," it says, in your own voice. "I am what you left behind. I have been keeping it warm. Some of it you might want back."

options.label: Reach for what was lost
options.outcome: You press your hand to its chest. There is pain, not wound-pain, but the specific pain of remembering who you were before you knew what you know now. When you pull back, the shade is gone. But something has returned, a vigor, a readiness, the kind that only comes from knowing exactly what you are fighting for.
options.chronicle: Met myself from before the descent. I was cleaner. I did not envy me.

road.hint: Who you were is not waiting to be reclaimed.

options.label: Reject the reflection
options.outcome: The shade tilts its head. "You have become someone that the old you would not entirely recognize," it observes, without judgment. "That is not a tragedy. That is the whole point." It dissolves like mist struck by a beam of light and you are alone with your reflection in the wet stone floor.

options.label: Walk through it
options.outcome: It offers no resistance, you pass through cold air and a brief cascade of half-remembered smells: a specific kitchen, a specific rain. You do not look back. The shade, if it watches, says nothing.

name: Death
text: A chessboard on a rock, and at it a pale man in a black hood who is not a man. Behind you, a juggler, his wife and a baby are hiding behind their painted cart, very still. "I am Death," he says, as if apologising. "They're mine tonight. So are you, eventually. Will you play? I always offer." He sets out the pieces. "Your years are the stake. Name what you play for."

options.label: Play for the family, staking your own years

pass.outcome: He studies the board for a long time, and knocks his king over himself, carefully, as if it mattered to get it right. "They may go." Behind you the cart creaks away down the road, and the baby laughs at something.
pass.chronicle: Played Death at chess for a juggler's family and won. He knocked over his own king, carefully. The baby laughed as the cart went.

fail.outcome: He takes your pieces one by one, and with them a little of your years. Then he stands, and goes round the cart, quite gently. The masks on the cart turn to watch him go by.
fail.chronicle: Played Death at chess for a juggler's family and lost. He took some of my years, and then them, gently. I staked what I had. It was not enough.

road.hint: A game played for someone else is never wholly lost.

options.label: Play for yourself, staking the same years

pass.outcome: "Well played." He makes a small mark in a small book. "On the way home with your Stone, I will give you back one breath I would have taken. Once."
pass.chronicle: Played Death at chess for my own life and won a breath back from him, for later. The juggler's family did not get a game.

fail.outcome: He takes your years and the family both.
fail.chronicle: Played Death at chess for my own life and lost. He took my years, and the juggler's family, who had not been asked to play.

road.hint: Some winnings are counted in other people's losses.

options.label: Offer him the family if he lets you pass
options.outcome: He looks at you for a long time, and then he nods, and goes round the cart. You do not look back. Behind you, the little bells on the cart stop ringing.
options.chronicle: Offered Death a juggler's family to let me pass. He took them. He looked at me first, for a long time, in a way I keep thinking about.

road.hint: A trade with Death always costs the other party.

options.label: Walk away
options.outcome: "Another time," he says. "There is always another time, until there isn't."

name: Dim Light in the Stone
text: A crack in the wall pulses with warm golden light, too rhythmic to be fire, too alive to be stone. When you lean close, you feel the heat of something enormous pressed into a space far too small for it. A voice comes from within the crack: "Smaller than I was. But not gone. Traveler, I can offer you something, if you offer something in return."

options.label: Lay your bare hand on the stone
options.outcome: The stone sears your palm and the light surges, briefly, brilliantly. "There," says the voice, with something like relief. "That was nourishing. I had nearly forgotten what living things feel like." A warmth travels up your arm and spreads, and you feel your body begin to quietly, persistently knit itself together.
options.chronicle: Laid my hand on a crack where something enormous was pressed into a space too small for it. It was warm, and grateful.

road.hint: Something very large can be very small for a while.

options.label: Offer your mana to the trapped god
options.outcome: The magic leaves you in a slow, warm exhale, drawn into the stone like breath on a cold day. "Ah. Old power. Thank you." A long pause, then: "I am too diminished to repay you as I once could. But take this, the least I have to offer." The warmth returns, settling into your wounds, sealing them.

options.label: Press on without engaging it
options.outcome: The light dims as you pass, like eyes closing. "Another time, perhaps," says the voice, with a patience that has been accumulating for longer than civilizations. You feel the light watching you long after the crack is out of sight.

name: Kneeling Herald
text: A man in the black and yellow of the Locust's heralds kneels in the middle of the corridor with his hands up and his banner thrown down. "Sanctuary. I'm done with them. I know where the Destroyer is weak, and I'll tell you everything, only hide me." He keeps glancing back up the corridor. His shadow lies the wrong way, toward the torch.

options.label: Hide him in the side passage and hear him out
options.warning: His shadow lies the wrong way, toward the torch.
options.outcome: He thanks you, and weeps, and while you are watching the corridor for pursuers he puts a knife in your back and runs to fetch them.
options.chronicle: Gave sanctuary to a herald of the Locust who said he had changed sides. He had not. I should have looked at his shadow.

road.hint: A shadow that falls toward the torch belongs to no honest man.

options.label: Ask him how he got past the pickets, and keep asking

pass.outcome: He came past the eastern pickets at dusk, he says. Then it was the western ones, at the change of the watch. Then there were no pickets, because he is a herald and they let heralds through. You let him hear the three stories side by side. He hears it too. He runs, and a folded paper falls out of his sleeve: his real orders, naming the place he was to lead you, which you will now go round.
pass.chronicle: Let a herald who wanted sanctuary tell me how he got past the pickets three times. It was three different stories. He dropped his real orders running.

fail.outcome: His story holds together as far as you can follow it.
fail.chronicle: Questioned a herald about his escape and could not find the crack in it. The knife found me instead.

road.hint: A true story told three times stays the same story.

options.label: Turn him away
options.outcome: He gets up, dusts himself off, picks up his banner, and walks back the way he came without any hurry at all.
options.chronicle: Turned away a herald of the Locust who begged for sanctuary. He walked off in no hurry at all. I think I was right.

road.hint: A man fleeing for his life does not stroll.

options.label: Strike him down where he kneels
options.outcome: He is up and fighting before your blade lands, with a speed no penitent has.
options.chronicle: Struck down a kneeling herald before he could finish his story. He was quicker than any penitent. I am still not proud of how I knew.

road.hint: Being right by luck teaches nothing.

name: Disreputable Imp
text: A small, red, deeply self-satisfied creature sits atop a crate with 'DEFINITELY FINE GOODS' stenciled on the side in handwriting that changes between letters. It points at you with a claw the size of a needle and announces: "YOU. You look like someone with gold and poor decision-making skills. Perfect. PERFECT. I have things."

options.label: Buy something from his definitely-fine crate
options.outcome: He produces something from the crate with theatrical effort, requiring both arms and one foot. "Finest quality! Mostly! The cursed ones are in the OTHER crate and I DEFINITELY didn't mix them up this time." He takes your gold and bites it experimentally. "Acceptable."
options.chronicle: Bought something from an imp's crate labelled DEFINITELY FINE GOODS. The handwriting changed between letters.

road.hint: Handwriting that changes between letters is a confession.

options.label: Ask what's actually in the crate
options.outcome: He stares at you. Then at the crate. Then back at you. "...Conceptually? Hope." He pauses. "Physically? I'm not entirely sure anymore. Something shifted on level ninety and I think the inventory reorganized itself on philosophical grounds." He looks genuinely concerned for a moment. Then the moment passes.

options.label: "No thank you, actually."
options.outcome: His face falls with operatic despair. "NO. No no no. Do you know how few people get to level eighty-something? Do you know how long I've been waiting?" He watches you go. "I'll be here!" he calls. "I am always here. I don't know how to leave!"

name: Medical Construct
text: A golem made of white stone stands in an alcove, its chest engraved with a serpent-and-staff symbol worn nearly smooth by centuries. It turns toward you with the careful movements of something built to handle fragile things. "SUBJECT ASSESSED: ALIVE. CONDITION: SUBOPTIMAL. SERVICES AVAILABLE. INDICATE REQUIREMENT."

options.label: Request wound treatment
options.outcome: It works with the impersonal efficiency of something that has been doing this for seven hundred years and finds it neither interesting nor tedious, it simply finds it correct. When it finishes, your wounds are sealed, your breathing is even, and it has left a small receipt in your pocket in a language that may not exist anymore.
options.chronicle: Paid a stone medical golem to patch me up. It assessed me as ALIVE. I appreciated the confidence.

road.hint: A healer built from stone does not flinch.

options.label: Request stamina treatment
options.outcome: It administers something it calls a "musculoskeletal optimization procedure," which involves exactly three minutes of targeted pressure to specific points that you didn't know you had. You feel the deep exhaustion of eighty-some floors drain out of you like water from a wrung cloth.

options.label: "I am fine. Thank you."
options.outcome: It processes this for a moment. "ASSESSMENT INDICATES STATEMENT INACCURATE. HOWEVER: PATIENT AUTONOMY PROTOCOLS APPLY." It steps back into its alcove. "SAFE TRAVELS, SUBJECT." It says this with something that sounds, against all probability, like it means it.

name: Berengar the Gold
text: A towering warrior slumps against the wall, his golden armor shattered, a dozen wounds weeping light rather than blood. "I made it to the ninety-second floor once," he rasps, "before the thing with a thousand mouths found me. I won't make it further. But you, you still have breath in you."

options.label: Give him 200 gold for funeral rites
options.outcome: He shakes his head when you offer coin, but you press it into his hands anyway. He looks at it for a long moment, then presses his sword hilt to yours. "Take the edge from Berengar's blade. Let it taste whatever lies below." Your weapon gleams with new purpose.

options.label: Sit with him a while
options.outcome: You say nothing. He says nothing. The silence between you is the companionship of people who understand what this place costs. When he finally stills, you feel something settle over you, a dying man's final wish for another's survival. You feel blessed.
options.chronicle: Sat with a dying hero who once reached the ninety-second floor. He told me what found him there.

road.hint: The last hero to come this far left a warning, if you sit long enough.

options.label: Keep moving, there is no time
options.outcome: He doesn't blame you. He just watches you go with eyes that have seen too many things walk past. You hear him whisper something as you round the corner, a name, perhaps, or a prayer.

name: Ortolan the Last Merchant
text: A stout man in a coat with too many pockets sits on a chest that radiates unnatural warmth, counting coins that seem to disappear between his fingers before being counted again. "Ortolan's Emporium, deepest shop in the world, est. longer than you've been alive!" he announces cheerfully. "What'll it be?"

options.label: Buy something from his stock
options.outcome: He rummages through the chest with alarming depth, his arm disappears to the shoulder before he produces something with a triumphant grunt. "Finest stock this side of the abyss! Probably. I stopped checking labels after level sixty."
options.chronicle: Bought from the deepest shop in the world. Ortolan says he has always been here. I believe the prices, at least.

road.hint: The last shop charges what the last shop can.

options.label: Buy a scroll from him
options.outcome: He produces a scroll with a flourish, sealed with wax in the shape of a coin. "Knowledge, the only currency that appreciates!" he says. "That's something a customer told me. I mostly just sell things."

options.label: "How do you survive down here?"
options.outcome: He taps the side of his nose. "Good prices and fast feet, friend. The monsters leave me alone because I give them favorable terms on bulk purchases." He winks. You cannot tell if he is joking. You strongly suspect he is not joking.

name: The General Out of Time
text: A man in ancient armor stands at perfect attention, studying a battle map drawn on the floor in chalk that does not smudge. His army, you realize, is indicated by a single mark. He looks up at you with the bright, slightly too-focused eyes of someone who has been waiting a very long time. "Soldier! Report. What is the current strategic situation?"

options.label: Play along and give him a "report"
options.outcome: You invent a battle. He listens with furious, grateful attention, making marks on his map, nodding at your fabrications as though they confirm long-held suspicions. "Good. Then the third flank must move." He grips your arm with a general's certainty. "Double-time, soldier. I'll buy you a moment." You feel your feet lighten.

options.label: Tell him the truth gently
options.outcome: He listens. His face does the complicated thing faces do when time catches up with them all at once. Then he straightens his shoulders. "I see. Then I have been standing guard over nothing." A pause. "No. Not nothing. I have been standing." He presses his rations into your hands. "Take these. Your war is not yet over."

options.label: Salute and move on
options.outcome: He returns the salute with crisp, unbroken discipline. "At ease, soldier." You walk past his chalk army and his chalk enemy and his single chalk mark, and you do not look back, because some things deserve the dignity of an unwitnessed vigil.

name: Weeping Prophet
text: A woman kneels in the center of the corridor, tears streaming freely, though her expression is serene rather than anguished, the face of someone who has made peace with being ignored. "I know what you will face," she says. "I know what you will choose. I have said so many times, to so many people, and none of them believed me until it was done."

options.label: "Tell me anyway. I will listen."
options.outcome: She looks at you with an expression that is the entire history of being taken seriously for the first time. She speaks quickly, like someone who knows the window might close. The words wash over you and sink in, and for a time the dungeon holds no secrets from you.

options.label: Offer her food to restore her strength
options.outcome: She takes the food with both hands and eats with the careful gratitude of someone who has forgotten how it tastes. "You fed a prophet," she says softly. "The old texts say something about that. Something good." She touches your cheek, and you feel the world tilt slightly in your favor.

options.label: "Prophecy is a burden I cannot share."
options.outcome: "Yes," she says simply. "I know." She watches you go with the patient, ruined dignity of someone who has been correct about everything and helped no one. The sound of her weeping does not follow you. You almost wish it did.

name: Keeper of Last Memories
text: A robed figure sits surrounded by softly glowing motes, hundreds of them, drifting like embers from a dying fire, each one pulsing with its own quiet warmth. "Each of these," it says without turning, "is the last thought of someone who did not make it back. I keep them so they are not simply lost. You may carry one, if you choose."

options.label: Accept a fallen adventurer's last memory
options.outcome: The mote settles on your palm and dissolves. For a moment you are someone else, someone who died on level ninety-four, who knew exactly where the shadow-thing waited, who almost made it. The knowledge they died for is yours now. You feel the weight and the gift of it equally.
options.chronicle: Accepted the last memory of someone who did not make it back. It was of a kitchen, and somebody laughing.

road.hint: The last thought of the fallen is usually of home.

options.label: Leave a memory of the surface world here
options.outcome: You concentrate on something bright, a morning, a meal, a face, and it lifts gently away and joins the other motes. The Keeper watches it go. "Thank you. The collection is heavy with endings. It is good to add something that felt like a beginning." The loss settles into you strangely, like a wound that has been given proper care.

options.label: Observe the motes in silence and move on
options.outcome: You stand for a moment among the last lights of the lost. The Keeper does not press you. The motes drift around you without touching, as though they sense you are still using yourself. When you go, you feel them watching you with something that is almost hope.

name: Roland
text: A pass between black rocks, and the dead of a rear guard lying where they held it. One knight is still sitting up against a stone, blood on his temples, an ivory horn in his lap and a sword across his knees without a mark on it, and beside him a great rock split clean in two, as if a sword had been beaten against it. "Roland," he says. "Oliver told me to blow it. Three times." He holds out the horn. "Too late now for them. Blow it at the Black Gate, where they'll hear it above. So the rear guard is remembered."

options.label: Swear to blow it at the Black Gate
options.outcome: He puts it in your hands. "Oliver was right," he says. "Wisdom and courage. He had both. I had only one of them." He closes his eyes.

oath.what: Blow the Olifant at the Black Gate, so the rear guard is remembered.

thread.hint: An ivory horn is waiting to be blown at the Black Gate.

options.chronicle: Took Roland's horn and swore to blow it at the Black Gate for the rear guard. He said Oliver had been right, three times.

road.hint: A horn not blown in time can still be blown in memory.

options.label: Blow it here, now, for him
options.outcome: You blow it, and the note goes up the pass and away. Nothing answers; it is far too late for answers. Roland smiles anyway. "There," he says. "That's what it sounds like." He dies listening to the echo.
options.chronicle: Blew Roland's horn for him in his pass, far too late to bring anyone. He smiled and said that was what it sounded like.

road.hint: Some calls are made only so the caller can hear them.

options.label: Take Durendal from him
options.outcome: He tried to break it rather than let an enemy have it. He has no strength left to stop a friend. He watches you lift it. "Carry it well, then," he says, "since I couldn't break it."
options.chronicle: Took Durendal off a dying Roland. He had tried to break it on a rock so no enemy would have it. He did not have the strength to stop me.

road.hint: A sword its master tried to break is still loyal to someone.

options.label: Ask him why he didn't blow it
options.outcome: "Because a knight of France doesn't call for help against heathens," he says. "That's what I said. Oliver said a brave man who throws away his army is no wiser than a coward." He coughs. "He was right. Write that down."

name: Boethius
text: A cell with the door open, and inside, an old man in a senator's toga gone grey writes by a single lamp. He does not leave. "Theodoric's men come when the watch changes," he says, without looking up. "The door? I could walk out. But I'd be running from a lie, and I'd rather finish the book." He sets down the pen. "Tell me. A man who loses everything Fortune gave him: is he poorer?"

pass.outcome: "Then Fortune never gave him anything that was his," you say. "Only lent it." He laughs, delighted, like a teacher whose worst student has finally got there. "That is my second book, Fortune and her wheel. You've saved me a chapter."
pass.chronicle: Answered Boethius's question in his cell. He laughed and said I had saved him a chapter. They come for him when the watch changes.

fail.outcome: He nods, kindly. "That is where I was, a month ago. It gets better."

road.hint: What Fortune gives, she lends. What you know, she cannot take.

options.label: "Walk out with me. The door's open."
options.outcome: "I know," he says gently. "That's why it's open. Go on. I want to finish the last line before the light goes."
options.chronicle: Offered to walk Boethius out of an open cell. He said that was why it was open, and went back to his last line.

road.hint: Some men stay in an open cell because leaving would say the lie was true.

options.label: Sit with him in silence
options.outcome: He writes. You sit. Once he reads you a sentence and you nod, and he crosses it out anyway.

name: Sir Oswin
text: A pilgrim sits on the stair with his boots off, rubbing his feet. "The knight from Thale? Big man, cracked holy symbol?" He points up the way you came. "He passed me going up, singing. Badly. Said he was going home to testify against his bishop."

text_variants.text: A heap of dead demons fills a crossroads, more than you can count, and on top of it, like a man who fell asleep on a hill, lies Sir Oswin, his cracked holy symbol in his fist.

options.label: Ask the pilgrim about the knight
options.outcome: "Singing," says the pilgrim again, as if that were the strange part. "All the way up. I'd not have thought a man that size could climb that fast."
options.chronicle: A pilgrim on the stair passed Sir Oswin going up to testify against his bishop and give Thale back. He said the knight was singing.

road.hint: Some debts are paid where everyone can see.

options.label: Close his eyes
options.outcome: The blessed armour is warm under your hand. It let him wear it again, at the end.
options.chronicle: Found Sir Oswin dead on a hill of demons. His armour had forgiven him, I think. I closed his eyes.

road.hint: Atonement down here is measured in heaps.

options.label: Walk on
